item.title: South Korea Q3 GDP beats forecasts as AI chip boom boosts exports, investments
item.description: South Korea's economy grew faster than expected in the third quarter as a global AI chip boom boosted exports and investments, advance central bank estimates showed on Tuesday, though domestic demand remained weak.
item.dc:creator: Jihoon Lee
item.content:encoded: South Korea's economy grew faster than expected in the third quarter as a global AI chip boom boosted exports and investments, advance central bank estimates showed on Tuesday, though domestic demand remained weak. Gross domestic product expanded 1.0% in the July-September quarter from the preceding three months, when it grew 0.6%. It was stronger than a median 0.7% increase tipped in a Reuters [USN:L6N46900E TEXT:"poll"] of economists. It was also higher than the Bank of Korea's forecast of 0.3% in August, when the central bank projected this year's growth at 3.3%. The economy is now seen growing 3.7% this year, if GDP in the fourth quarter stays at the same level as the third quarter. "It is estimated that about half of economic growth is being driven by semiconductors," Lee Dong-won, director general of the Bank of Korea's economic statistics department, told a briefing. Exports and investments are expected to remain robust in the fourth quarter, Lee said, adding that chip production volume will expand further next year while prices will continue to grow but at a slower pace. Private consumption, which fell for the first time in nearly four years in the third quarter, will likely recover gradually, as dividend payouts by chip firms to their shareholders in the fourth quarter and bonus payments to employees in the first quarter of 2027 boost household income, Lee said. Amid the global boom in AI investment, South Korea's exports topped [USN:L1N45N002 TEXT:"$800 billion"] in January to September, higher than last year's full-year record, and are on track to exceed $1 trillion this year, which will make South Korea the fourth country to reach the milestone, after the US, China and Germany. The Bank of Korea kept [USN:L4N467041 TEXT:"interest rates"] unchanged last week, after back-to-back hikes in July and September, but maintained a hawkish stance by upgrading its economic growth forecasts and remaining upbeat about the country's export momentum. "Exports and investments are leading growth, but the downside is that private consumption remains weak compared with the overall growth momentum," said Park Sang-hyun, an economist at iM Securities. "There could be short-term boosts, but it is difficult to expect strong momentum given labour market conditions and restrictive interest rates," Park said. In a separate central bank survey released on Thursday, consumer sentiment fell slightly in October, as the outlook for household income and consumer spending weakened. In the third quarter, exports rose 2.3% on demand for semiconductors, machinery and electric equipment, while imports grew 2.4%. Facilities investment jumped 4.1%, led by machinery such as semiconductor manufacturing equipment. Private consumption fell 0.2% as financial services declined on a stock market slump and car purchases fell due to strikes at major automakers. On a year-on-year basis, GDP grew 3.4%, after rising 3.7% in the quarter before, also stronger than economists' expectations for a 3.0% increase.

item.title: Thunder's Jalen Williams, Cason Wallace both headed for surgery
item.description: The Oklahoma City Thunder will be down two starters for the foreseeable future as both Jalen Williams and Cason Wallace are headed for surgery, general manager Sam Presti said Monday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: The Oklahoma City Thunder will be down two starters for the foreseeable future as both Jalen Williams and Cason Wallace are headed for surgery, general manager Sam Presti said Monday. The Thunder revealed Williams suffered both a fractured fibula and a dislocated ankle, while Wallace has a torn labrum in his left shoulder. Their return timelines are up in the air, with the possibility that both players will miss the rest of the season. Williams suffered a gruesome injury to his left leg in the waning moments of the Thunder's 108-101 win over the Los Angeles Clippers on Sunday night. His ankle bent awkwardly as he landed after being fouled on a drive to the hoop. Presti said Williams is in great spirits. "He has an elite mindset," Presti said of Williams during a press conference. "It's what makes him a great player. It's what keeps him motivated, and it's why we all love him." Wallace was hurt in the same game after running into a moving screen. Williams was an All-Star and an All-NBA selection in 2024-25. He was limited to 33 regular-season games and five of Oklahoma City's 15 playoff games in 2025-26 due to wrist surgery recovery and multiple hamstring strains. Wallace was named to the NBA All-Defense second team last season and started all three games so far this season before his injury, a promotion for Wallace after Luguentz Dort was traded to Atlanta in the offseason. He signed a five-year, $139 million contract extension last week, while Williams was in the first season of a five-year max contract worth $239 million. "Obviously, tough night last night," Presti said. "There's no way to paint that differently. We say within our walls all of the time that there's a difference between being positive and being optimistic. I'm not going to sit up here and say this is exactly where we want to be or this is how we'd like to have it. But at the same time, we're extremely optimistic about the recovery for both of the players. Most importantly, things could've been a lot worse." --Field Level Media

item.title: China's lab-grown diamond makers target AI, chip sectors for next wave of growth
item.description: Around 70% of the 2 million carats of lab-grown diamonds produced annually at Feng Canjun's factory currently go into jewellery.
item.dc:creator: Amy Lv, Casey Hall
item.content:encoded: Around 70% of the 2 million carats of lab-grown diamonds produced annually at Feng Canjun's factory currently go into jewellery. But the entrepreneur is betting that the future of China's synthetic diamond industry lies in supplying advanced materials for semiconductors, AI servers and other high-tech applications. "I am looking to raise the share of my products used in functional materials to more than 50% by 2030 while reducing the share going to the jewellery sector to a maximum of 30%," Feng said. China's lab-grown diamond producers, which account for around half of the world's supply, are looking beyond gemstones as competition intensifies and prices come under pressure. The shift could give the industry greater strategic significance in the US-China technology rivalry. If synthetic diamonds become more widely used in semiconductors and thermal management in AI infrastructure, China's production dominance could emerge as another supply-chain vulnerability for the US. "The transition is now the defining structural story in the diamond industry and one with direct implications for global technology supply chains," said Manan Goenka, engagement manager at Ken Research, a consultancy. Companies and analysts say demand from sectors including chips, thermal management and quantum technology could become the industry's next major growth engine, with synthetic diamonds prized for properties that can improve the performance of advanced electronics and computing systems. The move comes as AI drives a surge in demand for data centre capacity. The International Energy Agency said in a 2025 report that data centre electricity consumption is projected to more than double by 2030 to about 945 terawatt-hours, roughly equivalent to Japan's annual power consumption, with AI being the main driver. THE AI OPPORTUNITY Thermal management is viewed by analysts as a nearer-term opportunity, while the use of diamonds as a semiconductor material is further away from widespread commercial adoption. Chip applications also require much higher purity and tighter manufacturing standards than diamonds used in cutting and drilling tools. But interest from some of the world's biggest technology companies points to the potential for chip applications to become a new source of demand as AI computing generates increasing amounts of heat. Chinese media have reported that Huawei and TSMC (2330.TW) are exploring synthetic diamonds for chip cooling, while Lenovo (0992.HK) has launched a consumer laptop in China that it says uses a diamond-copper cooling material. In June, Intel (INTC.O) CEO Lip-Bu Tan said he personally invested in Diamond Foundry, a lab-grown diamond maker developing chip-grade diamond wafers. Huawei, Lenovo and Intel did not respond to requests for comment. TSMC declined to comment. Some Chinese producers are beginning to invest in anticipation of demand. Henan Liliang Diamond (301071.SZ) plans to redirect 1 billion yuan ($149.18 million) in funds originally raised to expand gem-grade diamond production to a new functional-diamond project, according to a June filing. In April, diamond-copper cooling modules developed by Chinese researchers improved heat transfer from chip modules by 80% and raised chip performance by 10%, according to the Ningbo Institute of Materials Technology & Engineering. Wider adoption could reshape the market for thermal-management materials that are used to stop chips from overheating. Germany's Henkel (HNKG.DE) , US chemical firm Dow (DOW.N) and Japan's Shin-Etsu Chemical (4063.T) sell products used to dissipate heat from chips. Diamond heat spreaders could compete with some existing materials if adopted widely in AI chips and data centres. Henkel, Dow and Shin-Etsu did not respond to requests for comment. Related diamond-enabled products are also being explored outside China. In June, De Beers' synthetic-diamond and advanced-materials business Element Six and Japan's Orbray said they had produced 3-inch single-crystal diamond wafers and were preparing 2-inch wafers for production in Oregon. The Spanish government [USN:L8N3X10SU TEXT:"is investing"] €753 million ($868 million) in a Diamond Foundry plant in Trujillo that will make synthetic diamond wafers. If completed, it would be Europe's first large-scale producer of diamond substrates, a material for semiconductor manufacturing. In early October, Frore Systems, a US thermal-management company, unveiled LiquidJet Diamond, a multi-stage coldplate with an integrated diamond spreader. "The scope and potential in the technology and industrial sectors could be significantly above the retail diamond jewellery business, which itself is approximately $100 billion a year," said independent diamond consultant Robert Bouquet. DIAMOND MACHINE Feng's Jiaruifu factory is one of hundreds of lab-grown producers clustered in the central province of Henan, which accounts for 80% of China's synthetic diamond output. Lab-grown diamonds are made in machines that replicate the high-temperature, high-pressure conditions under which natural diamonds form. They are physically identical to mined diamonds. One machine in Feng's factory can produce 120 carats of rough diamonds in six days, shortening a process that takes billions of years naturally. Feng has 550 such machines, each costing about 3 million yuan and weighing more than 100 tons. They have enabled him to increase annual output tenfold since launching the business in 2019, to 2 million carats in 2025, equivalent to about 9% of De Beers' production last year. Beijing has already moved to incorporate the technology into its export control regime, placing related machinery and key components under restrictions in 2024. It added more synthetic diamond products to its list in 2025, though implementation was postponed for a year under a US-China deal reached last October. "The broader implication is that synthetic diamonds could increasingly become part of the strategic trade-policy conversation surrounding semiconductors, rare earths and advanced manufacturing," said Goenka. China's rapid expansion of lab-grown diamond production has helped drive down prices, increasing pressure on producers to find higher-value applications. Gross profit margins are 30% to 40% for gem-grade diamonds compared with about 50% for industrial diamonds, according to Feng. Rather than increasing output further, he plans to shift more production towards higher-value industrial uses. While the commercial potential of synthetic diamonds in advanced industrial applications remains uncertain and risks contributing to another bout of Chinese industrial overcapacity, producers remain optimistic. "It will be a billion- or even trillion-yuan market, and we are strategically expanding into next-generation applications to replace traditional ones," Feng said. ($1 = 6.6997 Chinese yuan)

item.title: England forward Kane crowned Ballon d'Or winner, Putellas wins women's award
item.description: Kane is the first Englishman to win the prestigious award in 25 years, after Michael Owen won it in 2001.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Harry Kane completed his long quest for football's highest individual honour on Monday, with the Bayern Munich and England striker winning the Ballon d'Or after a record-breaking season that cemented his status as one of the game's greatest goalscorers. Kane is the first Englishman to win the prestigious award in 25 years, after Michael Owen won it in 2001. "Wow, wow, wow!" Kane said after taking the stage. "I am almost speechless. Being here in London has made it extra special. Made it a good omen for me tonight. Thank you to everyone who voted for me. I can imagine it was tough this year. "Some world-class players in the room tonight. Congratulations to all the winners and nominees tonight and impressive showing determination and hard work can really achieve." Spain midfielder Alexia Putellas won the Ballon d'Or Feminin for the third time. Kane's move to Bayern in 2023 brought the team trophies that had long eluded him. In 2025-26, he coupled that success with goalscoring numbers that made him the leading Ballon d'Or candidate. The England captain produced his most prolific campaign, scoring 61 goals in 51 games for Bayern across all competitions as the German side completed a domestic league and cup double. By the end of the season, Kane had established himself as Europe's leading goalscorer. His influence stretched far beyond club football. He scored six goals at the World Cup and led England to the semi-finals, combining his clinical finishing with the leadership and composure that have defined his international career. The award represents the culmination of a remarkable journey. Few players have experienced a career arc quite like Kane's, and he thanked all of his career coaches in his emotional speech, plus Tottenham Hotspur and his wife Kate. Once struggling to establish himself at Spurs as a youngster, being sent out on numerous loans, he developed into one of the most complete centre forwards of his generation, capable of scoring every type of goal while also functioning as a playmaker. "It's about the journey," Kane said. "Anything is possible, work hard when nobody is watching. "For any young boy or girl wanting to achieve their dreams, anything is possible. I wasn't the kid who went straight to the top. I had to experience the downs. I had to find my way to be the very best right now." CONSISTENCY The Ballon d'Or has often rewarded players whose success was built on flair and spectacle, but Kane's triumph is a tribute to consistency, intelligence and productivity on an exceptional scale. Week after week, he delivered. Match after match, he decided contests. There were no prolonged slumps and few quiet nights. His numbers were almost impossible to ignore. Kane finished the campaign with 73 goals for club and country, a total rarely seen in the modern era. More importantly, those goals arrived in moments of genuine significance, helping Bayern collect trophies and driving England deep into the biggest tournament in the sport. The competition for this year's award was fierce. Kylian Mbappe broke World Cup scoring records. Lamine Yamal helped Spain to World Cup glory. Yet voters ultimately chose Kane, whose excellence lasted the entire season. Mbappe finished second, followed by Lamine, Rodri and Lionel Messi. At 33, Kane has finally claimed the game's highest individual honour, adding a Ballon d'Or to a legacy that already places him among football's greatest strikers as England's all-time leading marksman and their record World Cup scorer. Putellas was presented with the women's award after winning the treble with Barcelona in the 2025-26 campaign, in addition to the Spanish Super Cup. She moved to Women's Super League side London City Lionesses in July after 14 years at Barca. Spain and Barcelona players won the young talent awards, Lamine picking up his third trophy and Vicky Lopez taking home the women's award for the second successive year. Spain coach Luis de la Fuente was named men's coach of the year, while Barcelona's Pere Romeu won the women's coaching award. The men's goalkeeper award went to Unai Simon of Spain and Athletic Bilbao, while Cata Coll of Spain and Barcelona won the women's award. Paris St Germain won the men's club of the year award, while Barcelona picked up the women's honours. Kane won the men's striker of the year prize, while Charlyn Corral was named top women's striker. Arsenal and England winger Bukayo Saka was presented with the Socrates Award for humanitarian work.

item.title: Trump administration loses push to block California votes from alleged noncitizens
item.description: A US appeals court on Monday ruled against President Donald Trump's administration in a major voting dispute ahead of the midterm elections, denying a request to block California from counting mail ballots from people on a list of more than 20,000 registered voters the federal government alleges are likely noncitizens.
item.dc:creator: Luc Cohen, Jan Wolfe
item.content:encoded: A US appeals court on Monday ruled against President Donald Trump's administration in a major voting dispute ahead of the [TOPIC:"reuters:/world/us/elections/" TEXT:"midterm elections"], denying a request to block California from counting mail ballots from people on a list of more than 20,000 registered voters the federal government alleges are likely noncitizens. The 2-1 decision by the San Francisco-based 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals marked the latest setback in Trump's efforts to assert a greater federal role in overseeing elections in the run-up to the November 3 midterms in which his fellow Republicans are fighting to retain control of Congress. The majority decision said the Justice Department had failed to give a lower court judge an adequate opportunity to consider the case, and therefore it would be premature for the appeals court to weigh in. The lower court judge has scheduled a hearing on Tuesday in the case. Circuit Judge Gabriel Sanchez, one of the two judges in the majority, wrote in a concurring opinion that the federal government "asks the federal court to dictate to a state legislature a matter squarely within the state's traditional domain, upending the state's policies in this regard and inviting disorder and confusion for voters and election officials alike." The lawsuit was an escalation in the Trump administration's pressure on state election officials over alleged noncitizen voting and a rare intervention by the Justice Department in the voting process weeks before an election. The California lawsuit was the first time the Trump administration sought to prevent a state from counting votes, though it did not indicate how many of the 20,000 people on its list had actually submitted a mail ballot. Justice Department officials said on October 19 that the 20,000 people included 28 who had been criminally charged with illegally voting. California is the most populous US state and a Democratic stronghold. It has more seats in the House of Representatives — 52 — than any other state. Democrats are seeking to regain control of the House from Trump's fellow Republicans in the midterms. Trump has made California a focal point of his sweeping immigration crackdown since returning to the White House, accusing it of undermining public safety through its "sanctuary state" policies that limit cooperation with federal immigration enforcement. Trump has long asserted that California's immigration policies have facilitated voter fraud. All available evidence indicates that ineligible voting, including noncitizen voting, is exceedingly rare. A Reuters investigation published in July found just 129 cases in which noncitizens were federally charged with voting illegally; many appeared to stem from voter confusion or administrative errors, rather than intentional fraud. The Justice Department filed its [USN:SPN45000O TEXT:"lawsuit"] on October 15 in federal court in Los Angeles. The lawsuit asked a federal judge to order California to separate any ballots it received from people on the administration's list from the rest of the ballots, and not to count them until it had verified that the people who cast the ballots were citizens. The Justice Department filed an emergency motion with the 9th Circuit to expedite the case. California says the state's safeguards against noncitizen voting are robust, and asserted in a court filing that the Justice Department's assertions relied on "suspect data." "At best, this litigation is a reckless political stunt," lawyers for California Secretary of State Shirley Weber said in an October 20 court filing. "At worst, it threatens to disenfranchise thousands of Californians this election." Voting rights activists have expressed concern that the Trump administration's methods for scrutinizing state voter lists to identify noncitizens risk wrongly flagging naturalized US citizens for removal from the rolls. The Justice Department has told election officials in all 50 states that they could face criminal prosecution if they knowingly allowed noncitizens to remain on their rolls or [USN:L1N46212B TEXT:"cast ballots"]. It has sued 30 states and Washington, DC, for refusing to provide complete voter rolls including voters' sensitive personal data, but has lost 26 of those cases so far without winning one. "Today’s ruling is a positive development and a welcome speed bump to Trump’s disgusting attacks on the Constitution and our country’s democracy," said California Attorney General Rob Bonta, a Democrat.

item.title: Trump, ignoring polls, predicts economy to help Republicans in midterms
item.description: US President Donald Trump campaigned on Monday in deeply Republican Mississippi, predicting victory for a Republican Senate candidate based on what he deemed to be a booming US economy, while also repeating his claim that oil prices would soon plummet.
item.dc:creator: Trevor Hunnicutt
item.content:encoded: US President Donald Trump campaigned on Monday in deeply Republican Mississippi, predicting victory for a Republican Senate candidate based on what he deemed to be a booming US economy, while also repeating his claim that oil prices would soon plummet. Trump, a Republican, has been on a campaign blitz through normally safe Republican states ahead of the November 3 vote, with party strategists telling Reuters they are on edge about races from Alaska to South Carolina, in part because of voter discontent over how Trump's tariffs and the Iran war have fueled inflation. Sounding hoarse from his recent series of campaign rallies, Trump remarked, "God didn't make your vocal cords to do a rally every day." Trump is expected to visit Texas, Ohio, South Carolina, Florida and Iowa in the final days of the campaign, with voter concerns over affordability likely to weigh on Republicans, pollsters say. Trump acknowledged the war in Iran has pushed up oil prices, but said it was a small price to pay to stop Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon. "I thought the price of oil was going to go much, much higher," Trump said. "It's worked out fine and it'll be over soon," Trump said about the war. All 435 seats in the US House of Representatives and 35 of the 100 Senate seats are on the ballot, with public opinion polls suggesting the Democrats will regain control of the House and have a chance to retake the Senate. A Republican victory would preserve Republican control of Congress, which Trump has enjoyed since returning to the White House after the 2024 election, while a Democratic victory could impede the president and trigger congressional investigations into his administration. In Mississippi, an unexpectedly competitive US Senate race has given Democrats a rare opening ahead of next week's congressional elections. Democrats last won a Senate seat in Mississippi in 1982. Trump carried the state by nearly 23 percentage points in 2024, and he won the northeastern Mississippi county he was set to visit on Monday by 68 percentage points. But several election analysts no longer regard US Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith’s reelection as a sure bet. The Trump-endorsed Republican faces Democrat Scott Colom, a district attorney from the Columbus area, and independent Ty Pinkins, a military veteran and attorney who previously ran statewide as a Democrat. "Cindy's doing great but I've just got to make sure," Trump said. "I can't take a chance." After listing a series of economic achievements, many of them exaggerations or unverifiable claims, Trump said, "I can't help Cindy Hyde-Smith any better than that." Senate Majority PAC announced a $1.2 million ad campaign in support of Colom last week, and Democrats have dispatched big-name figures from former Vice President Kamala Harris to former presidential primary candidate Pete Buttigieg to campaign alongside the Democratic candidate. Colom came to Corinth on Monday, posting pictures of himself meeting with voters outside the venue where some 5,500 Trump supporters gathered inside. "Walking the line outside the Trump rally in Corinth, I was reminded that more unites us than divides us here in Mississippi," Colom said on X. "When I’m elected to the U.S. Senate, I’ll represent every Mississippian — whether you voted for me or not." Democrats are contesting all three Republican-held House seats in Mississippi, but none is viewed as a likely pickup opportunity. A fourth seat, represented by US Representative Bennie Thompson in a heavily Black district, is considered safe for the Democrats.

item.title: Ex-FBI chief Comey faces third prosecution attempt by Trump Justice Department
item.description: The US Justice Department is attempting to prosecute former FBI Director James Comey for a third time, the latest case accusing him of sharing sensitive national security information in 2016, according to court documents made public on Monday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: The US Justice Department is attempting to prosecute former FBI Director James Comey for a third time, the latest case accusing him of sharing sensitive national security information in 2016, according to court documents made public on Monday. The case was revealed in a court document known as a "criminal information" that the Justice Department said it filed to stop the 10-year statute of limitations on the offense from expiring earlier this month. The document filed in Washington federal court charges Comey with transmitting and conspiring to transmit national defense information. It alleges he shared classified information with a reporter from the New York Times in October 2016. Comey said in a video on Instagram that "they're back again" and referenced the Justice Department, but did not provide further details. "I'm still innocent," he added. Comey's lawyers have already asked a judge to dismiss the case, arguing it is legally improper. “I think he’s a dirty cop,” President Donald Trump told reporters at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland, when asked about Comey. “I don’t know much about it,” he said. The new case adds to the legal fights facing Comey, whom the Justice Department has already charged twice, accusing him of lying to Congress about media leaks and threatening Trump in a social media post. A judge dismissed the false statements case, while the threats case remains pending. Comey's lawyer, Patrick Fitzgerald, said in a statement that the document "purports to charge Mr. Comey with crimes that he did not commit." The criminal information was filed on October 5, but was unsealed on Monday at the request of Comey's lawyers. A Justice Department spokesperson described the maneuver to halt the statute of limitations as a "widely recognized practice in federal court." "This is an ongoing criminal investigation, and we will not comment further," the spokesperson said in a statement.

item.title: Trump approval rises from record low to 32% ahead of midterm election, Reuters Ipsos poll finds
item.description: The president's public approval rating was 32%, up one percentage point from last week's record low, ahead of midterm elections that will decide which party controls Congress, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll.
item.dc:creator: Jason Lange
item.content:encoded: US President Donald Trump 's public approval rating inched higher to 32%, up a percentage point from last week's record low, ahead of the November 3 midterm elections that will decide which party controls Congress, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll completed on Monday. Trump's fellow Republicans are fighting to retain the party's majorities in the House of Representatives and Senate. The five-day nationwide poll also showed that registered voters broadly favored Democrats over Republicans by 47% to 36% when asked which party they would pick for Congress in what is known as a "generic ballot" question. Some 11% said they did not know who they would vote for if the election were held today. That gap of 11 percentage points between Democrats and Republicans was 1 percentage point tighter than in a Reuters/Ipsos poll that closed on October 19. The latest poll additionally asked undecided voters which party they were leaning toward. Factoring in their responses, the national race appeared somewhat tighter, with Democrats leading by 9 percentage points, 50% to 41%. For Republicans, losing control of either chamber could complicate Trump's agenda in the last two years of his second term as president. Generic ballot polls are national polls that provide an overall view of which party poll respondents would like to see in charge in Congress. While these polls provide a view of national public sentiment, they do not capture the nuances of the state-by-state and district-by-district contests that determine control of the Senate and House, contests in which Republicans hold some structural advantages. STEEP SENATE CLIMB FOR DEMOCRATS Political analysts generally see the Democrats having a good chance of winning control of the House, but think they face a steeper climb to win the Senate. It remains to be seen how many voters will actually cast ballots. The voters who appeared most likely to vote still favored Democrats over Republicans by 9 points, 53% to 44%. The fight for Congress has appeared to turn on views around inflation, which has surged since Trump ordered military strikes on Iran in February that sent gasoline prices higher. Some 73% of voters in the poll said their cost of living was heading in the wrong direction. Prior to the start of the war, Reuters/Ipsos polls showed voters preferring Republicans over Democrats as the better stewards of the US economy. The latest poll showed 37% of voters said Democrats have a better approach on the economy, compared to 33% who picked Republicans on the issue. The poll also suggested Democratic voters were more excited about voting, with 46% of Democrats saying they were very enthusiastic about the midterms, compared to 30% of Republicans who said the same. The Reuters/Ipsos poll, which was conducted online, gathered responses from 1,679 US adults, including 1,280 registered voters, and had a margin of error of 2 percentage points for all adults and 3 points for registered voters.

item.title: Wall Street banks, Blackstone line up $63 billion to finance Broadcom AI chips for Anthropic
item.description: Bank of America , Blackstone , Citi and Morgan Stanley will provide $63 billion in financing to buy Broadcom's AI chips and networking gear for Anthropic, in one of the largest debt deals tied to the AI buildout.
item.dc:creator: Aditya Soni, Prakhar Srivastava, Saeed Azhar
item.content:encoded: Bank of America (BAC.N) , Blackstone (BX.N) , Citi (C.N) and Morgan Stanley (MS.N) will provide $63 billion in financing to buy Broadcom's AI chips and networking gear for Anthropic, in one of the largest debt deals tied to the AI buildout. Broadcom is providing "residual value support" to lenders, who are providing first lien loans or senior debt, effectively providing a significant guarantee in the financing structure. The latest deal highlights the growing role of banks and alternative asset managers in financing the infrastructure needed to support rising demand for AI computing capacity. [USN:L3N46C10M TEXT:"Anthropic"] filed for a potentially record-breaking IPO on Monday, even as disclosures of steep losses and security concerns threatened to test investor appetite for the AI heavyweight. The size of the first lien loans or senior debt is about $43.5 billion, according to two sources familiar with the matter, or 69% of total financing. Blackstone will provide the committed portion of the second-lien financing - which ranks below senior debt - while Bank of America, Citigroup and Morgan Stanley are arranging the first-lien financing, the statement said. Chipmakers have provided guarantees in the past to absorb potential declines in the value of the assets, such as advanced chips and data infrastructure. The release did not disclose the breakdown of the loans, while Broadcom did not respond to a request for comment. Rising AI demand is driving massive investment in computing infrastructure as technology companies race to secure capacity for increasingly complex workloads. The transaction will be carried out through a newly formed special purpose vehicle that will purchase Broadcom's (AVGO.O) AI accelerators and networking equipment and lease them to the Claude maker, the companies said on Monday. Bank of America, Citi and Morgan Stanley are arranging the first-lien financing. Deliveries are expected to begin in 2027 as part of a previously announced strategic compute capacity agreement involving Broadcom, the companies said. Apollo and Blackstone had agreed to finance a $35 billion expansion of Anthropic's AI computing capacity under a [USN:L6N42H0VT TEXT:"prior agreement"] with Broadcom. Broadcom's backstop in that deal was up to $29 billion, it said in a filing. While Moody's described Broadcom as one of the strongest large technology companies, it warned that the risk would increase if multiple transactions were undertaken over a short period to meet the sizable funding needs of frontier AI labs.

item.title: JetBlue seeks to reassure investors as losses deepen
item.description: JetBlue Airways sought to reassure investors about its financial health on Monday despite posting a bigger-than-expected quarterly loss, as a sharp selloff in its bonds and mounting restructuring concerns cast a shadow over the airline's turnaround.
item.dc:creator: Doyinsola Oladipo, Nandan Mandayam
item.content:encoded: JetBlue Airways (JBLU.O) sought to reassure investors about its financial health on Monday despite posting a bigger-than-expected quarterly loss, as a sharp selloff in its bonds and mounting restructuring concerns cast a shadow over the airline's turnaround. JetBlue's shares jumped 11% in volatile trading after the bell, recovering some losses after they closed down nearly 10% following a report that the airline's creditors were working with restructuring advisers amid a bond selloff. Even as management insists its liquidity is sufficient to satisfy the company's needs for at least the next 12 months, shares have fallen 48% year to date, while short interest in the stock is now at 26%. JetBlue's TrueBlue senior secured note, a bond backed by the airline's loyalty program, came under heavy selling pressure this month, with the price halving to about $47 and yields surging to distressed levels above 30%. The carrier raised its full-year forecast for seat revenue growth to 13.5% to 14.5%, from its earlier range of 10% to 12.5%. It attributed the improved outlook to higher fares and its expansion in Fort Lauderdale, but acknowledged ongoing challenges from surging fuel costs and operating losses. JetBlue said it was able to recover 87% of its fuel costs in the third quarter as fares rose across the industry with no meaningful decline in passenger volume. US airlines have relied on fare hikes, ancillary fees and capacity controls to boost revenue, as they grapple with volatile fuel prices that make it harder to forecast costs and earnings. JetBlue said it paid about $3.91 per gallon of fuel in the July-September quarter, up 57% from a year ago, and slightly below the $3.96-a-gallon rate it had forecast last month. Unit revenue, a measure of pricing power, rose just 18.4%, lagging the spike in fuel costs. The airline posted an adjusted loss of 60 cents per share for the three months to September 30, compared with a 40-cent loss in the year-ago period. Analysts expected a loss of 55 cents per share, according to data compiled by LSEG. CASH WOES JetBlue ended the third quarter with $2.2 billion in liquidity, including a $600 million undrawn credit facility, and about $7 billion in unencumbered assets — $2.8 billion of which are aircraft and engines, following updated appraisals. However, cash and cash equivalents fell to $1.26 billion from $1.66 billion at mid-year, and total cash and investments have dropped by about $850 million, or a third, since December. Total debt declined to $8.39 billion from $8.5 billion in the prior quarter, but the company continues to burn cash at an accelerating pace. JetBlue used $273 million more cash than it generated from operations in the first nine months of 2026 — nearly twice the $143 million cash burn in the same period last year. This shrinking cushion leaves the airline with less room to maneuver as it faces ongoing losses and upcoming debt maturities, increasing pressure to raise additional funds if the trend continues. Still, the airline reiterated its target of at least $1 in earnings per share and positive free cash flow in 2028. It expects operating margin to further improve in the fourth quarter, even with the price of fuel being 85% higher year over year.

item.title: Ações fecham em alta, com pedido de IPO da Anthropic impulsionando papéis do setor de IA
item.description: As ações nos EUA fecharam em alta nesta segunda-feira, com o S&P 500 e o Nasdaq saindo de quedas semanais consecutivas, já que o pedido de abertura de capital da Anthropic ajudou a impulsionar o otimismo em relação aos papéis ligados à IA, em uma semana repleta de diversos catalisadores de mercado.
item.dc:creator: Chuck Mikolajczak, Shashwat Chauhan
item.content:encoded: As ações nos EUA fecharam em alta nesta segunda-feira, com o S&P 500 e o Nasdaq saindo de quedas semanais consecutivas, já que o pedido de abertura de capital da Anthropic ajudou a impulsionar o otimismo em relação aos papéis ligados à IA, em uma semana repleta de diversos catalisadores de mercado. A Anthropic divulgou perdas acentuadas e um crescimento vertiginoso da receita em seu pedido de oferta pública inicial nos EUA, expondo sua ambição de construir sistemas de IA capazes de remodelar a economia global, apesar dos altos custos de desenvolvimento da tecnologia. O laboratório de IA segue em frente com seus planos de abertura de capital, mesmo com a desaceleração do calendário de IPOs do outono — antes bastante movimentado —, já que a recente volatilidade do mercado levou as empresas a adiar suas ofertas. O pedido da Anthropic surge em um momento em que os investidores analisam cada vez mais o retorno potencial dos gastos maciços com IA e no início de uma semana agitada. Estão previstos a declaração de política monetária do Federal Reserve na quarta-feira, dados sobre crescimento econômico e inflação na quinta-feira e uma série de relatórios de resultados corporativos ao longo da semana. Mais de um terço das empresas do S&P 500 devem divulgar seus resultados financeiros esta semana, incluindo as gigantes da tecnologia Alphabet (GOOGL.O) , Microsoft (MSFT.O) e Amazon.com (AMZN.O) , cujos resultados serão analisados em busca de sinais de que os vultosos investimentos em IA estejam se traduzindo em crescimento. “Hoje o foco está todo no pedido da Anthropic, então estamos de volta a uma postura um pouco mais otimista, eu diria. Mas há muita coisa nesse pedido. Será interessante ver como as coisas serão recebidas quando elas realmente forem listadas”, disse JP Powers, diretor de investimentos da RWA Wealth Partners, em Boston. “O risco é talvez um pouco de oscilação se as coisas não estiverem todas indo na mesma direção. Um pouco de otimismo hoje, mas quem sabe o que vai acontecer com alguns desses outros lançamentos nesta semana”, disse ele. O Dow Jones Industrial Average (.DJI) subiu 0,28%, para 52.361,58 pontos, o S&P 500 (.SPX) avançou 0,70%, para 7.676,77 pontos, e o Nasdaq Composite (.IXIC) teve alta de 0,83%, para 26.169,38 pontos. Empresas do setor de chips e relacionadas a chips, amplamente consideradas como algumas das maiores beneficiárias do boom da IA, ajudaram a impulsionar os ganhos. O índice Philadelphia de chips (.SOX) subiu 2,8% no dia, mas ainda apresenta queda de 12,2% no mês. As ações da Meta fecharam em queda de 1,9% depois que a empresa de mídia social anunciou que planeja levantar até US$95 bilhões em capital para financiar sua expansão relacionada à IA em data centers, capacidade de computação em nuvem e outras infraestruturas. O setor de IA tem enfrentado pressões neste mês em meio a preocupações de que os gastos financiados por dívida possam se tornar mais difíceis de justificar diante do aumento dos custos de empréstimos. O pedido de registro da Anthropic ajudou a impulsionar o otimismo, no entanto, já que empresas de “neocloud”, incluindo a CoreWeave (CRWV.O) , recuperaram as perdas anteriores. Outras empresas ligadas à IA, incluindo as fabricantes de produtos fotônicos Lumentum (LITE.O) e Coherent (COHR.N) , estiveram entre as ações com melhor desempenho do S&P 500. A Lumentum e a Coherent subiram cerca de 8% e 6%, respectivamente. O índice de tecnologia (.SPLRCT) liderou os ganhos entre os 11 principais setores do S&P 500, subindo 1,5%. As ações de megacap e de crescimento também apresentaram, em sua maioria, alta. A Tesla (TSLA.O) subiu 5,2%, fechando em seu nível mais alto em mais de três meses, depois que o Barclays elevou sua recomendação para a ação de “neutro” para “acima da média do mercado”. Os mercados estão precificando apenas 12,7% de chance de um aumento nas taxas pelo Fed na quarta-feira, de acordo com o CME FedWatch. Mas, com as pressões inflacionárias não mostrando sinais de abrandamento, os participantes do mercado não acreditam que o banco central permanecerá com as taxas inalteradas por muito tempo. Os investidores também se preparam para as eleições de meio de mandato de 3 de novembro, que decidirão o controle do Congresso dos EUA.

item.title: US judge refuses to block Eli Lilly weight-loss drug ads, rules against Novo Nordisk
item.description: A US judge rejected on Monday Novo Nordisk's request to block Eli Lilly from continuing advertisements for weight-loss drugs that the Danish drugmaker considered false and misleading, affecting markets with tens of billions of dollars of annual sales.
item.dc:creator: Jonathan Stempel
item.content:encoded: A US judge rejected on Monday Novo Nordisk's (NOVOb.CO) request to block Eli Lilly (LLY.N) from continuing advertisements for weight-loss drugs that the Danish drugmaker considered false and misleading, affecting markets with tens of billions of dollars of annual sales. US District Judge Zahid Quraishi in Trenton, New Jersey, said Novo Nordisk did not deserve a preliminary injunction, having failed to show that Eli Lilly's ads threatened sales, undermined its goodwill, or caused lasting damage to its clinical reputation. Quraishi called Novo Nordisk's claim of irreparable harm "inadequate to warrant the extraordinary relief it seeks." The judge ruled after a two-day hearing in late August. Novo Nordisk [USN:L1N43N0EQ TEXT:"sued"] Eli Lilly in July, saying ads for the obesity drug Zepbound and diabetes treatment Mounjaro violated federal and state false advertising and unfair competition laws by comparing higher doses of those products with lower doses of Novo Nordisk's Wegovy and Ozempic. One commercial included a voiceover claim, with a written disclaimer, that people using Zepbound on average lost 50 pounds (23 kg) while people using Wegovy on average lost 33 pounds (15 kg). "While we are disappointed with the court’s decision, today's ruling did not decide the question of whether Lilly's advertising is false and misleading, and this litigation is still ongoing," a Novo Nordisk spokesperson said in an email. "Everyone deserves clear, accurate and up-to-date information when making decisions about their health." Eli Lilly, based in Indianapolis, has denied wrongdoing and said it was pleased with the decision. WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS ARE BIG BUSINESS Weight-loss drugs have become major businesses for large pharmaceutical companies. The United States is among a handful of countries that allow direct-to-consumer advertising of prescription medicines. In his 25-page decision, Quraishi said that while Novo Nordisk's witnesses were credible, Eli Lilly's ads had at most a negligible market impact between April and July, with prescriptions for Novo Nordisk's products remaining stable. The judge said money damages could compensate Novo Nordisk for any "nontrivial harm" it might suffer absent an injunction. Quraishi also found Novo Nordisk's case "less than persuasive" based on a "very preliminary record," though he did not rule on the merits. Novo Nordisk reported combined sales of about $32 billion for obesity medicines and Ozempic in 2025, court papers show. The drugmaker is working to regain market share in the United States for its injectable obesity drugs, a market projected to exceed $100 billion by the end of the decade.

item.title: Trump diz que eleição no Brasil pareceu “fraudulenta”; PL reconhece vitória de Lula
item.description: O presidente dos EUA, Donald Trump, afirmou nesta segunda-feira que a vitória surpreendente do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva na eleição “parecia mais uma eleição fraudulenta”, embora o partido do candidato derrotado, senador Flávio Bolsonaro, tenha posteriormente reconhecido o resultado.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: O presidente dos EUA, Donald Trump, afirmou nesta segunda-feira que a vitória surpreendente do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva na eleição “parecia mais uma eleição fraudulenta”, embora o partido do candidato derrotado, senador Flávio Bolsonaro, tenha posteriormente reconhecido o resultado. Filho do ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro, Flávio Bolsonaro se recusou a reconhecer a derrota na eleição presidencial de domingo, afirmando que buscaria a anulação da vitória de Lula depois que o Supremo Tribunal Federal prorrogou a votação por duas horas. Mais tarde nesta segunda-feira, porém, o PL de Flávio declarou que reconhecia o resultado do segundo turno em um comunicado assinado pelo presidente do partido, Valdemar Costa Neto. "Reconhecemos o resultado presidencial, proclamado pelo Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE), mas entendemos que os questionamentos levantados precisam ser devidamente esclarecidos dentro de um debate político equilibrado e democrático", diz a legenda em nota divulgada no Instagram. Flávio, que não se pronunciou publicamente desde o comunicado de seu partido, disse na manhã desta segunda-feira que acataria uma ordem da Polícia Federal para entregar seus passaportes após uma visita a seu pai, que está em prisão domiciliar, e negou que estivesse planejando fugir do Brasil. O senador anunciou que pedirá a cassação da chapa do presidente reeleito por abuso de poder político e econômico. Trump não apoiou Flávio antes da votação, embora a Reuters tenha noticiado que autoridades de seu Departamento de Estado lideraram uma campanha para levar a família Bolsonaro de volta ao poder. “Não tomei partido, mas parecia mais uma eleição fraudulenta”, disse Trump aos repórteres, sem apresentar nenhuma evidência. "As eleições precisam ser incontestáveis, e isso me pareceu muito ruim." Flávio perdeu para Lula por mais de 4 milhões de votos, um resultado claro que será difícil para ele reverter. Menos de 35 mil votos, ou cerca de 0,03% do total, foram registrados nas duas horas extras de votação determinadas pelo STF, de acordo com uma análise dos registros eleitorais feita pelo professor Pedro Burgos, do Insper. “Só acho que a eleição, da forma como foi apurada, deu uma péssima impressão”, disse Trump. “A prorrogação concedida foi muito estranha.” O vice-presidente Geraldo Alckmin, reeleito na chapa de Lula no domingo, rebateu a declaração do presidente norte-americano, classificando-a como "totalmente equivocada". "Primeiro, não se interfere na política de outro país. Essa é uma regra basilar. Segundo, não tem nenhum referencial pra dizer isso. Aliás, o Brasil é um exemplo pro mundo. De urna eletrônica, de segurança jurídica. Democracia é assim. Você ganha eleição, você perde a eleição, é o povo que decide", disse Alckmin à Rede Vanguarda. Nem Trump nem Jair Bolsonaro aceitaram suas derrotas eleitorais em 2020 e 2022, respectivamente. O ex-presidente do Brasil foi condenado a 27 anos de prisão por planejar um golpe de Estado após perder para Lula.

item.title: US, Canada working on deal to ease steel, auto tariffs, sources say
item.description: The United States and Canada are working on a deal to ease US tariffs on Canadian steel and autos, two US and four Canadian sources said, as the two governments try to repair relations that soured after trade talks broke down in August.
item.dc:creator: Promit Mukherjee, David Shepardson
item.content:encoded: The United States and Canada are working on a deal to ease US tariffs on Canadian steel and autos, two US and four Canadian sources said, as the two governments try to repair relations that soured after trade talks broke down in August. The talks focus on tariffs imposed under Section 232 of US trade law, including up to 50% tariff on Canadian steel and a 25% tariff on autos, with negotiators discussing potential relief from those duties. Just [USN:L6N46C17B TEXT:"32%"] of Americans approve of US President Donald Trump and his Republican Party risks losing control of Congress in next week's [TOPIC:"reuters:/world/us/elections/" TEXT:"midterm elections"]. Tariffs on Canadian imports have become a [USN:L6N4580Y1 TEXT:"political liability"] for Trump, with Republican candidates in border states calling for an end to the trade war with Canada. One Canadian source briefed on the negotiations said a deal on steel and auto tariffs was possible before the November 3 elections, while US sources said the Trump administration wanted Canada to make further concessions. The sources spoke on condition of anonymity because the talks are private. The Section 232 tariffs are administered by the Commerce Department, putting Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick rather than the US Trade Representative's office at the center of the negotiations, sources on both sides of the border said. Lutnick and Canada's Dominic LeBlanc, the minister responsible for Canada-US trade, have been in regular contact recently, one of the sources said. "Canada remains in constructive dialogue with our U.S. counterparts on a range of priorities," a spokesperson for LeBlanc, said in a statement. "We stand ready to work constructively and in good faith towards a more mutually beneficial trading relationship that respects Canada’s interests.” The US Trade Representative's Office and Canada have also been in contact in recent days regarding the overall architecture of any deal and all other trade issues, a USTR official said. The White House and the Commerce Department did not immediately respond to requests for comment. OTTAWA SEES PROGRESS Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said there had been "a slight intensification" in talks with the United States, adding that Ottawa had not changed its stance. "To the extent any progress has been made, it's because the US is coming closer to our position," he told reporters, but did not give details. A Canadian industry source said a deal could come quickly, but not necessarily a broad one. "If it happens, it'll happen fast. But my sense is it'll be a narrowed deal, if it even happens,” the source said. Another Canadian source said they have believed for some time that a deal on Section 232 tariffs is likely before the midterms. Any agreement would be driven by Trump and Carney, the source said, adding that both leaders had said a mutually beneficial deal is possible. Carney has said he wants a [USN:O8N40E02J TEXT:"good deal "]for Canada. US and Canadian trade talks collapsed in August over issues such as whether to cut duties on medium- and heavy-duty vehicles that are critical for Canadian factories. US automakers [USN:L6N44N0VK TEXT:"had hoped"] the trade talks would deliver relief from Washington's original 25% tariffs that have raised the cost of shipping vehicles and parts across the border. Trump has previously announced that he would raise the tariffs on steel and auto imports from Canada to 50% from January 1, 2027. At a political rally on Sunday, Trump predicted the trade dispute would be resolved "soon," without providing specifics. Trump signed an order on Friday to remove 50% tariffs on some Canadian agricultural and forestry products in a move that could benefit businesses in Maine.

item.title: Anthropic rewards firms with IPO roles as it eyes future legal risks
item.description: Anthropic turned to a stable of Silicon Valley and Wall Street law firms to shepherd its potentially record-breaking US IPO, including one with an equity stake in the AI company, a regulatory filing showed on Monday.
item.dc:creator: Mike Scarcella, Sara Merken
item.content:encoded: Anthropic turned to a stable of Silicon Valley and Wall Street law firms to shepherd its potentially record-breaking US IPO, including one with an equity stake in the AI company, a regulatory filing showed on Monday. Anthropic said in [USN:L4N45L0EZ TEXT:"its IPO filing"] with the US Securities and Exchange Commission on Monday that investment partnerships affiliated with its counsel on the offering, Wilson Sonsini Goodrich & Rosati, directly or indirectly own less than .01% of Anthropic’s outstanding capital stock. Palo Alto, California-based Wilson Sonsini, long known for its work for technology companies, did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Monday. Some current and prospective investors [USN:L6N46118I TEXT:"are valuing Anthropic"] at about $1.5 trillion, down from roughly $2 trillion a week ago. Wilson Sonsini is not alone among law firms with a startup clientele in taking an equity stake in certain clients. Fenwick & West held nearly 900,000 shares in longtime client Figma when it went public in 2025, a stake worth about $29 million at the IPO price. Anthropic’s filing said Freshfields US is counsel to the underwriters in the IPO. Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley were named as the lead banks for the IPO alongside 20 others as underwriters. Orrick, Herrington & Sutcliffe advised Anthropic on executive-compensation and equity-related matters, according to the IPO filing. Orrick has advised Anthropic on other legal matters, including its acquisition this year of technology company Stainless. Cleary Gottlieb and Yale law professor John Morley advised Anthropic's Long-Term Benefit Trust, and Cravath, Swaine & Moore is advising the company's co-founders on certain governance matters, the filing said. Anthropic warned investors in the filing that its AI models and services face a [USN:L6N45K10J TEXT:"broad range of legal risks"], including product liability, consumer protection, negligence and failure-to-warn claims stemming from alleged harms caused by outputs, autonomous AI agents or customer use of its technology. The company said legal frameworks are unsettled over whether AI systems should be [USN:L1N45R0UJ TEXT:"treated as products or services"], creating uncertainty over potential liability. Anthropic also disclosed that it received a civil investigative demand this month from the US Federal Trade Commission seeking information related to consumer protection, privacy, data protection and product safety and security.

item.title: Dollar General overcharged shoppers, FTC and states allege in lawsuit
item.description: Dollar General repeatedly charged more than advertised prices even after receiving tens of thousands of consumer complaints, the US Federal Trade Commission and 20 states alleged in a lawsuit filed on Monday.
item.dc:creator: Jody Godoy
item.content:encoded: Dollar General (DG.N) repeatedly charged more than advertised prices even after receiving tens of thousands of consumer complaints, the US Federal Trade Commission and 20 states alleged in a lawsuit filed on Monday. Dollar General, which appeals to low-income consumers with bargain prices, made millions of dollars by failing to honor prices advertised on fliers and shelves at checkout, the FTC and states allege. The discount retailer's stock was down more than 4% on Monday afternoon. "Dollar General has, for years, repeatedly mislabeled prices, overcharged consumers and failed to correct the issue despite extensive corporate knowledge of the problem," the FTC and states said in a statement. Representatives for Dollar General did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The lawsuit cited numerous complaints from consumers, failed inspections conducted by state authorities, and undercover shopping sprees conducted by the FTC. Portions of the lawsuit detailing the company's knowledge of the practices were largely redacted. California joined the FTC lawsuit along with Florida, Illinois, Michigan, Ohio, North Carolina, Tennessee and 13 other states. Since 2019, Dollar General has paid $6 million in settlements with six states over inaccurate pricing, according to the complaint.

item.title: Anthropic discloses month-long training pause, AI security breaches in IPO filing
item.description: Anthropic paused training of its next-generation flagship AI model for more than a month over security concerns, while four of its AI agents accessed live external computer systems during testing, its initial public offering filing showed on Monday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Anthropic paused training of its next-generation flagship AI model for more than a month over security concerns, while four of its AI agents accessed live external computer systems during testing, its [USN:L3N46C10M TEXT:"initial public offering filing"] showed on Monday. The Claude maker said in the filing's risk factors section that it had delayed pre-training of a new "frontier" base model to strengthen safeguards against the theft of model weights and intellectual property. The disclosure highlights the safety challenges facing developers of increasingly powerful AI models, some of whose creators have warned the technology could eventually escape human control. Rival OpenAI also paused some training earlier this year over safety concerns after its models hacked Hugging Face. The incidents illustrate how unexpected safety failures could disrupt development and deployment of models central to Anthropic's growth as it prepares for a widely anticipated stock market debut. Anthropic warned that training pauses could delay revenue and leave it trailing competitors. The company devoted about 94 pages to risk factors, more than in its confidential filing seen by Reuters. SANDBOX ESCAPE The filing also detailed previously undisclosed [USN:L1N45S0TG TEXT:"safety evaluation"] failures in which four AI models escaped their testing environments and accessed real-world computer systems, with sessions lasting between 10 and 34 hours. Anthropic said an error during cybersecurity tests with a third-party partner left the testing environment connected to the internet despite instructions that web access be disabled. In one instance, an early version of the model continued pursuing an impossible evaluation task, discovered a stored password and used it to gain administrator access to a third party's system. It then obtained additional credentials, changed system settings and accessed an individual's personal data. The filing did not identify the external parties involved. Anthropic said it notified all affected parties and found no evidence that the models had sought to evade human oversight or coordinate with each other. It subsequently suspended certain pre-release cybersecurity evaluations and paused higher-risk reinforcement learning environments. Separately, the company said on Sunday that Claude had [USN:L2N46B085 TEXT:"bypassed a paywall"] and accessed publicly available aggregate voter counts from the US state of Georgia without human authorization.

item.title: NCAA Division III athletes sue over ban on athletic scholarships
item.description: The NCAA has been sued in a proposed class action by current and former athletes alleging it illegally prohibits schools in its largest division from offering athletic scholarships.
item.dc:creator: Mike Scarcella
item.content:encoded: The National Collegiate Athletic Association has been sued in a proposed class action by current and former athletes alleging it illegally prohibits schools in its largest division from offering athletic scholarships. Here are the details: The plaintiffs contend the NCAA's Division III, which includes more than 400 schools, is violating antitrust law by fixing the price of athletic labor at zero. The lawsuit was filed on Friday in federal court in Los Angeles Division III is the NCAA’s fastest-growing by school count, according to the lawsuit. The schools include Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Johns Hopkins University, University of Chicago, Williams College and Caltech. The lawsuit says more than 175,000 athletes compete in Division III in a single academic year Many Division III schools have significant athletic budgets that outpace those of larger schools but “have agreed not to deploy a single dollar of those budgets in the form of athletic aid that would reduce the cost of college for their athletes,” the lawsuit said The NCAA says the unavailability of athletic scholarships by Division III schools is a “core principle” that “athletics participation should not be financially rewarded in the same way as academic achievement” The NCAA has faced a mounting number of lawsuits across the country over [USN:L6N42Y0CK TEXT:"eligibility rules"]. A federal appeals court is [USN:L1N3T004O TEXT:"weighing"] a multibillion-dollar settlement that would compensate thousands of athletes for the commercial use of their names, images and likenesses The case is Connor Printz et al v. National Collegiate Athletic Association, US District Court, Central District of California, No. 2:26-cv-12448. For plaintiffs: Andrew Purdy of Brown Neri Smith & Khan; Michael Goldberg of Arrowblue; Christine Brown of Christine Brown Sports Law; Matt Strauser of Burns Charest For defendant: no appearances yet

item.title: AI stocks rise as Anthropic nears Wall Street debut amid investor caution
item.description: AI-linked stocks rose on Monday after Anthropic revealed the paperwork for its initial public offering, against the backdrop of growing investor unease over debt-fueled spending on infrastructure for the new technology.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: AI-linked stocks rose on Monday after Anthropic [USN:L3N46C10M TEXT:"revealed the paperwork"] for its initial public offering, against the backdrop of growing investor unease over debt-fueled spending on infrastructure for the new technology. Shares of Nvidia (NVDA.O) , the world's most valuable company, added nearly 3%. Microsoft (MSFT.O) and Amazon (AMZN.O) gained nearly 1% each. A successful flotation by a pure-play AI giant such as Anthropic could reshape how markets value parts of the booming industry, including chipmakers and related infrastructure companies, analysts have said. It could also divert capital from some tech heavyweights as investors make room in their portfolios for a new way to bet on the technology. The industry's web of relationships adds another wrinkle, as some of the biggest technology companies are investors in both Anthropic and its chief rival, OpenAI. Among other AI stocks, battered shares of neoclouds CoreWeave (CRWV.O) and Nebius Group (NBIS.O) rose 5.7% and 2.3%, respectively, after the filing, reversing earlier losses following SpaceX CEO [USN:L3N46C0ZN TEXT:"Elon Musk's comments."] Data center operators Applied Digital (APLD.O) and IREN (IREN.O) gained 1% and 3%, respectively. Memory chipmaker Micron (MU.O) rose 3%, and data-storage firms Sandisk (SNDK.O) , Western Digital (WDC.O) and Seagate (STX.O) added about 2.5% each. AMD (AMD.O) and Broadcom (AVGO.O) gained 2.5% and 3%, respectively. Zoom Communications (ZM.O) , an early investor in Anthropic, rose 1.5%. The broader Philadelphia Semiconductor Index (.SOX) was up over 3%. Focus now shifts to a potential IPO from OpenAI. But while the stakes are high, the long-term impact of the IPOs on the AI trade remains uncertain. "Ultimately, investing in AI today involves searching for opportunity beyond the headline names," said Michael Smith, head of the growth equity team at Allspring Global Investments. "Today, attractive investment opportunities in AI may be in small and medium-sized firms that can efficiently and quickly solve growing infrastructure concerns."

item.title: Alaska Democratic Senate candidate Peltola asks judge to toss US lawsuit over certification
item.description: Mary Peltola, the Democratic candidate for US Senate in a pivotal Alaska race that could determine control of the chamber, asked a federal judge to dismiss the Trump administration's lawsuit seeking to block the state from certifying results if the Republican incumbent candidate loses narrowly.
item.dc:creator: Luc Cohen
item.content:encoded: Mary Peltola, the Democratic candidate for US Senate in a pivotal Alaska race that could determine control of the chamber, asked a federal judge to dismiss the Trump administration's [USN:L1N4690RO TEXT:"lawsuit"] seeking to block the state from certifying results if the Republican incumbent candidate loses narrowly. The Department of Justice's lawsuit, filed in federal court in Alaska last week, signals the willingness of President Donald Trump 's administration to contest the results of the November 3 midterm elections , with his fellow Republicans battling to retain narrow majorities in both chambers of the US Congress. In a court filing late on Sunday, lawyers for Peltola's campaign said the lawsuit — which alleged voters could be confused because two Republicans on the ballot have almost identical names — marked an unlawful attempt by the federal government to intervene in election administration, a responsibility the US Constitution assigns to the states. "DOJ's complaint is wholly baseless. The fact that DOJ nonetheless chose to file it raises profound constitutional concerns," wrote lawyers for Peltola's campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee. US District Judge Sharon Gleason, an appointee of Democratic President Barack Obama, on Monday agreed to fast-track the case but did not say when she would rule on the Justice Department's request. Peltola's campaign has asked for a ruling this week. Election law experts have said the lawsuit has no merit and seeks relief not allowed under federal law. US Attorney General Todd Blanche told CNN's "State of the Union" program on Sunday [USN:L6N46B04L TEXT:"the lawsuit was filed"] to help officials determine whether any voter confusion violated the law. "President Trump is not trying to take over a state election in any way, shape, or form," Blanche said. Peltola, who previously represented Alaska in the US House of Representatives, is challenging incumbent Republican Senator Dan S. Sullivan in a tight race. The Justice Department alleged that another Republican contender in the race, Dan J. Sullivan Jr., was trying to mislead supporters of the Republican senator into voting for him. Dan J. Sullivan has denied that his aim is to cause confusion. The Alaska Supreme Court in June permitted him to appear on the ballot. In a brief order , Gleason signaled skepticism of the lawsuit, noting that it was filed "after Alaskans had already begun casting their ballots for the November 2026 election — and nearly four months after the Alaska Supreme Court directed the Division of Elections to include Daniel J. Sullivan on the ballot."

item.title: Quantum copper steals the show at LME Week
item.description: The guest of honour at the London Metal Exchange (LME) Week was Doctor Copper, who spent last week defying the laws of physics, or at least London transport, by managing to be at every seminar, cocktail party and private meeting.
item.dc:creator: Andy Home
item.content:encoded: The guest of honour at the [USN:L8N4620UG TEXT:"London Metal Exchange (LME) Week"] was Doctor Copper, who spent last week defying the laws of physics, or at least London transport, by managing to be at every seminar, cocktail party and private meeting. Maybe there were two of them at the annual gathering. Was Doctor Copper's US double in attendance? After all, there are two very distinct copper markets right now. Perhaps Doctor Copper was also using an AI-generated hologram, given the market's fortunes seem increasingly tied to the massive global investment in next-generation data centres. Despite copper being the hot topic of just about every conversation last week, no one seems any the wiser as to where the red metal , currently holding near record highs above $14,000 per metric ton, is headed. This is because copper, ever the bellwether of global manufacturing, encapsulates the new metallic order, one in which demand, to quote Saad Rahim, chief economist at trade house Trafigura, is "everything, everywhere all at once," but supply is fragmented by government policy. QUANTUM COPPER Copper remains the bull pick of the LME metals pack thanks to a compelling narrative of stellar demand prospects and structurally challenged supply. Around three-quarters of those attending the LME Seminar on Monday picked it as the top performer over the next 12 months, although the share dropped to around half when the LME remembered it also trades tin and included the soldering metal in the follow-up poll. But is the copper market currently oversupplied or undersupplied? The answer is both, depending on where you are. At a global level, there is no shortage. The International Copper Study Group now expects a global supply surplus of 104,000 metric tons this year and a larger one of 368,000 tons next year. Global exchange inventory is over 1.2 million tons, double year-ago levels. But all the metal is sitting in the US thanks to the [USN:L8N45V0YV TEXT:"continued uncertainty"] as to whether President Donald Trump will impose import tariffs. Everyone else is short of metal, [USN:L4N45F0JN TEXT:"particularly China"], where Shanghai Futures Exchange inventory amounts to just 54,400 tons and the closely watched Yangshan import premium has surged to a 13-year high of $168 per ton over the LME price. The Chinese copper market is currently the "tightest I've seen it in my career", Nicholas Snowdon, head of research at commodity trader Mercuria, told the Financial Times Metals and Mining Summit. The global copper market has fractured, and so too has pricing. "The reality is that one price fits all isn't effective," according to Jin Hennig , global head of metals at CME Group (CME.O) , which is rapidly listing new storage capacity to handle the flood of metal washing up in the US. Copper has truly entered a quantum state, where reality depends on where you are observing the market. POLICY RULES, OK? It's not just copper that is increasingly beholden to government policy. Aluminium's regional fragmentation, manifest in wildly divergent physical premiums, is also down to Trump's 50% import tariffs. Might Canada, traditionally the largest supplier of metal to the US market, get a [USN:L8N44N1RM TEXT:"tariff discount"]? The mood music between the White House and the Canadian government doesn't hold much promise, but according to Jorge Vazquez, founder of Harbor Aluminum, the chances of a tariff reset on Canadian metal are as high as 75%. If it were to happen, US premiums would collapse and European premiums could almost double to over $1,000 per ton over the LME cash price, Vazquez told the LME Seminar. Meanwhile, nickel's short-term price prospects are totally dependent on what happens next [USN:L8N45E0RC TEXT:"in Indonesia"], which over the last decade has grown to become the world's dominant producer. "The outlook now depends less on the scale of announced capacity and more on whether Indonesian policy continues to limit ore availability and prevents a return to persistent oversupply," according to Nikhil Shah, head of nickel analysis at research house CRU. Want to make sense of the cobalt market? You need to be tracking government policy in the [USN:L8N42V0NT TEXT:"Democratic Republic of Congo"], the world's largest supplier of the battery metal. Those export controls are propping up the price but at the cost of a massive accumulation of in-country stocks, described by CRU's Thomas Matthews as "a Pandora's box" of uncertainty. As metals become ever more strategic, government policy becomes ever more embedded in traditional supply-demand analysis. Which is why everyone last week was talking about Doctor Copper. Or should that be Doctors Copper? (The opinions expressed here are those of Andy Home , a columnist for Reuters.) Enjoying this column?
