item.title: Instant View: Anthropic IPO filing to put AI investment boom to the test
item.description: Anthropic made its US IPO filing public on Monday, edging toward what could be the first stock market debut by a frontier AI lab and laying out the promise, costs and risks of building AI meant to transform the global economy.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Anthropic made its [USN:L3N46C10M TEXT:"US IPO filing"] public on Monday, edging toward what could be the first stock market debut by a frontier AI lab and laying out the promise, costs and risks of building AI meant to transform the global economy. The IPO comes at a time when market volatility has thinned the fall listing calendar and rising borrowing costs have sharpened investor concerns over the debt-fueled AI investment boom. Wall Street's main indexes were higher in morning trade with the S&P 500 (.SPX) up 0.5%. U.S. stock index futures got a brief boost after the IPO filing. COMMENTS: JOSH STEVENS, CHIEF INVESTMENT OFFICER, CRESALTA INVESTMENT MANAGEMENT, COLORADO "I'm optimistic about AI as a technology. And Anthropic is certainly exciting. But are we going to rush in and buy at the IPO? No. Even great ideas or business models end up seeing their share prices come down to attractive levels during times when investors are reassessing demand and supply. And then, you've got an opportunity to go in and buy." PETER ANDERSEN, FOUNDER OF ANDERSEN CAPITAL MANAGEMENT, BOSTON "I think it's a significant milestone in the development of artificial intelligence. And the outcome of this IPO will be fairly indicative of the sentiment for continuing to support capital expenditures in the development of artificial intelligence." THOMAS HAYES, CHAIRMAN, GREAT HILL CAPITAL, NEW YORK "In the general sense of a business doing $16 or $32 billion annualized revenue, and losing $80 to $160 billion a year, a $1.5 trillion valuation seems rich. The offering is for the faithful, that sooner or later, they're going to get some return on that invested capital. The price could go up because they'll control the supply of stock that they issued, but in the long term, it's a weighing machine and losing that amount of money on that investment until they turn the corner, which is many years out, you'll have better places to buy it than at the initial public offering." "If people are raising cash for the Anthropic IPO with funds from the current hyperscalers in Mag Seven, that could be a headwind in coming weeks. It will be dependent on what we see in earnings from Microsoft, Alphabet, and Amazon this week." BRIAN MULBERRY, CHIEF MARKET STRATEGIST, ZACKS INVESTMENT MANAGEMENT, COLORADO"It'll be very interesting because Meta has come out and said we're going to raise another $95 billion in an equity offering as well, so you're going to have really a saturated market. There's a lot of liquidity that needs to get scooped up by these two offerings at the same time. I think it could be a detrimental to some of these smaller and maybe even lower quality AI names that are out there." LUKAS MUEHLBAUER, ASSOCIATE AT IPOX SCHUSTER, EDINBURGH "Anthropic’s IPO will certainly establish a benchmark for valuing leading AI labs, influencing both upcoming listings and confidence in the companies funding the AI infrastructure buildout." "Its success would not necessarily benefit every AI business equally, as investors will still distinguish between proven customer demand and spending based on anticipated growth." ANDRE BAKHOS, MANAGING MEMBER, INGENIUM ANALYTICS LLC IN PLAINSBORO, NEW JERSEY "It speaks a lot that the AI trade is alive and well. That the penetration of AI will continue. It also bolsters the psychology looking at the other participants in this space." "It's a race for capital and it's telling that there is growth. But also there are going to be questions coming in regarding valuations, regarding how long can this go for." ROBERT PAVLIK, SENIOR PORTFOLIO MANAGER, DAKOTA WEALTH IN FAIRFIELD, CONNECTICUT "It's a challenging environment, to say the least, exactly when this IPO will take place. There's a lot riding on not only the company, but the AI industry." "If it goes well, that could help return investors confidence to the AI industry. But it's going to be challenging." "Maybe the environment changes after the (US midterm) elections next week. You're going to have to make major promises that I don't know if they can be fulfilled anytime soon." MATT KENNEDY, SENIOR STRATEGIST AT RENAISSANCE CAPITAL "Investors weren't questioning valuations the same way a few months ago. With some of the hottest AI IPOs of the summer trading below their offer price, not even Anthropic will get a blank check." "Maybe they could have gotten a higher valuation next year, but they've decided to 'rip the band-aid off'." "For Anthropic, being publicly traded is also of strategic interest: This is a PBC (Public Benefit Corporation), and being publicly traded provides a greater level of public transparency."

item.title: Anthropic's IPO: A close look at AI frontrunner's rapid growth, spiraling costs
item.description: Anthropic unveiled its US initial public offering paperwork on Monday, setting up for a blockbuster market debut that would test investors' willingness to fund the AI juggernaut's bills amid growing worries over the massive debt-fueled spending.
item.dc:creator: Deborah Sophia
item.content:encoded: Anthropic [USN:L3N46C10M TEXT:"unveiled"] its US initial public offering paperwork on Monday, setting up for a blockbuster market debut that would test investors' willingness to fund the AI juggernaut's bills amid growing worries over the massive debt-fueled spending. The company had submitted a [USN:L4N4291D9 TEXT:"confidential filing"] in June. In the recent weeks, exclusive reporting from Reuters highlighted its [USN:L6N45L00I TEXT:"sweeping AI ambitions"], [USN:L4N4500J8 TEXT:"mounting costs"] and concerns about the "[USN:L4N45K1J5 TEXT:"existential risks to humanity"]" that advanced AI poses. Here are a few details on Anthropic's financials, business structure, and where it stands in the global AI race: BACKGROUND AND FINANCES Founded in 2021 by former OpenAI researchers including siblings Dario and Daniela Amodei, Anthropic is the startup behind the Claude family of AI models. Across four tiers - Fable, Opus, Sonnet and Haiku - Claude powers products such as Anthropic's chatbot, coding agent and the enterprise-focused Claude Cowork AI agent. Anthropic's early focus on training its models for coding tasks propelled the company to the forefront of the AI race and helped it draw a steady stream of enterprise customers. A majority of its revenue comes from businesses paying for its models per use, measured in "tokens" of information processed, in what Anthropic calls "consumption-based" revenue. It also generates revenue from its paid customer subscription tiers such as "Pro" and "Max". That has helped Anthropic grow its revenue to $4.59 billion in 2025 from $386 million a year ago and $41 million in 2023. For the six months ended June 2026, Anthropic's revenue was $16.29 billion, a massive increase from $1.16 billion for the same period in 2025. The company's operating losses have ballooned over the past years. But for the first half of 2026, they stood at $693 million, narrowing from $2.14 billion in the first half of 2025, as a fourteen-fold jump in revenue offset a fivefold increase in overall expenses. COSTS, COMPUTE DEMAND AND CIRCULAR AI INVESTMENTS Computing power is Anthropic's biggest expense. The company's costs include computing fees paid to cloud services providers such as Amazon Web Services and Google Cloud, costs tied to data center facilities and renting data center capacity, equipment leases and energy bills. Over the past three years, Anthropic's compute and infrastructure expenses have dwarfed its revenue. The company has committed more than [USN:L1N45K0RM TEXT:"$600 billion"] in spending with about eight partners over a decade - one of the largest AI buildout commitments on record. Anthropic said many portions of its agreements are non-cancelable or require payments regardless of usage. It has committed to spend at least $110 billion with Amazon (AMZN.O) , about $114.5 billion with Google (GOOGL.O) and $44.9 billion with Microsoft for cloud computing over the next seven to 10 years. But some of those companies are also its largest backers. Amazon and Google are among Anthropic's top shareholders, marking yet another example of the circular financing structures that have dominated capital flows in the AI industry. Amazon has invested at least $13 billion in Anthropic and has agreed to invest up to $20 billion more. Google has committed up to $40 billion to Anthropic. GOVERNANCE AND STRUCTURE Anthropic is a public benefit corporation, or PBC, meaning it is legally obligated to balance profitability goals for investors with developing AI for the benefit of humanity. An independent body elects a majority of its board. The company, helmed by Dario Amodei as CEO and his sister Daniela, as president and chair of the board, will continue to operate as a PBC after its listing. It expects to keep its founders and an independent trust in control, in a structure that could limit investor oversight and public shareholders' influence. The company has said it needs to concentrate control and capital in fewer hands to reduce AI's risks. Under this arrangement, a majority vote of its seven co-founders will direct a single share of Class F stock that amounts to 50.1% of the total voting power over key corporate matters, including the election of some board directors and other matters submitted to investors. COMPETITION Anthropic's most direct competitor is OpenAI, the creator of ChatGPT, whose 2022 launch kick-started the global race to adopt and advance AI technologies. Following Anthropic's lead in the enterprise market, OpenAI has sharpened its focus on products for developers and business customers. Anthropic is also locked in a race with Elon Musk's SpaceX, Alphabet's Google and Meta (META.O) . All of them are spending billions of dollars into model development, data centers and specialized AI chips as they vie for dominance in generative AI. Ramp data, which captures a slice of AI spending by business customers, showed Anthropic accounted for 60.1% of AI token spending in the week ended October 11.

item.title: From Amazon to Google, the deep-pocketed investors in Anthropic
item.description: Only a few startups have attracted as much investor conviction as Anthropic. Backed by some of the biggest names in technology and finance, the AI company has seen its valuation soar through successive funding rounds.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Only a few startups have attracted as much investor conviction as Anthropic. Backed by some of the biggest names in technology and finance, the AI company has seen its valuation soar through successive funding rounds. Its [USN:L3N46C10M TEXT:"initial public offering"] now offers a closely watched test of whether investors beyond Silicon Valley share that enthusiasm for the leaders of the AI boom. Here's a look at the key investors backing the Claude maker: Investor Details Amazon Amazon has invested at least $13 billion in Anthropic and in April agreed to invest up to an additional $20 billion. Anthropic also committed to spend more than $100 billion on the e-commerce giant's cloud services over 10 years Alphabet's Google Google has committed up to $40 billion to Anthropic, including an initial $10 billion investment announced in April. The partnership provides Anthropic with cloud infrastructure and access to Google's AI chips, which are used to train and run Claude models Spark Capital Spark Capital led Anthropic's $450 million Series C round in May 2023 and gained board representation through general partner Yasmin Razavi Lightspeed Venture Partners Lightspeed led the $3.5 billion Series E round in March 2025 and later co-led the $13 billion Series F round at a $183 billion valuation in September that year Fidelity Management & Research Fidelity participated in Series E and co-led the $13 billion Series F financing at a $183 billion valuation. The firm's other investments include Databricks and CoreWeave Salesforce Ventures Salesforce Ventures participated in the $450 million Series C round and the $3.5 billion Series E financing. The software firm's venture arm has also invested in firms such as Cohere and Chainguard ICONIQ Capital ICONIQ led the $13 billion Series F round at a $183 billion valuation and later co-led the $30 billion Series G financing. The venture capital firm's investments include OpenAI and smart ring maker Oura GIC Singapore's sovereign wealth fund led the $30 billion Series G round at a $380 billion valuation. GIC has also invested in AI voice generation startup ElevenLabs Coatue Management Coatue led the $30 billion Series G financing and later co-led the $65 billion Series H round. The investment firm has also financed companies such as Canva and CoreWeave D1 Capital Partners D1 Capital invested across multiple large financings including Series E, Series F, Series G and Series H. The firm has holdings in Cognition AI and SpaceX Sequoia Capital Sequoia was a significant investor in Series G and became one of the lead investors in the $65 billion Series H round at a $965 billion valuation Altimeter Capital Altimeter invested in the September 2025 $13 billion fundraise and was a lead investor in the $65 billion Series H financing at a $965 billion valuation Jaan Tallinn Skype co-founder Tallinn led Anthropic's first institutional financing, a $124 million Series A round in 2021. The angel investor has also funded open-source AI startup Zyphra and Rain AI Eric Schmidt The former Google chief executive has backed Anthropic personally and is among the company's best-known individual investors. Schmidt has also funded Yann LeCun's Advanced Machine Intelligence Menlo Ventures Menlo made its first investment in Anthropic in 2023 as part of a Series C round, and led Series D at an $18.4 billion valuation in 2024. It also participated in the $3.5 billion Series E round at a $61.5 billion valuation.

item.title: Egypt approves military support for Saudi Arabia after Houthi attacks escalate
item.description: Parliament authorised Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi on Monday to take "all necessary measures" to help Saudi Arabia defend itself — a move that could push Cairo more directly into the conflict between the kingdom and Yemen's Iran-allied Houthis.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Parliament authorised Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi on Monday to take "all necessary measures" to help Saudi Arabia defend itself — a move that could push Cairo more directly into the conflict between the kingdom and Yemen's Iran-allied Houthis. Sisi had [USN:L6N46403J TEXT:"asked parliament"] to approve military support for Egypt's Gulf Arab ally and the world's biggest oil exporter if Riyadh requested help in fighting the Houthis, whose advances also threaten the strategic [USN:L8N4520BL TEXT:"Bab el-Mandeb Strait"] — southern gateway to the Red Sea and Egypt's Suez Canal. At least two-thirds of the chamber backed the measure, according to an official parliamentary statement. Parliament voted in closed session without publishing the tally, and no formal Saudi request for Egyptian troops has been announced. The statement did not specify what kind of support Egypt would provide. Taher al-Khouly, deputy head of parliament’s legislative committee, told Reuters that Egypt would send forces to Saudi Arabia in coordination between the two countries and at Saudi Arabia’s request. Several opposition groups opposed or declined to back the move. The Civil Democratic Movement, a coalition of opposition parties, rejected Egyptian military involvement in a regional war and said last week that Cairo’s role should focus on mediation. The Egyptian Social Democratic Party had said its lawmakers would abstain, citing a lack of information on the mission’s aims, duration and cost, while saying it remained supportive of Saudi Arabia. Egypt has frequently condemned Iranian and Iranian-backed attacks on Gulf countries, but it has not publicly engaged in direct combat or joined the Mecca [USN:L1N45R0S7 TEXT:"mutual defence"] pact between Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey, [USN:L6N4440IT TEXT:"signed in August"]. Ministers from the pact’s member countries held an emergency meeting in Riyadh [USN:L1N45R0S7 TEXT:"earlier this month"] and agreed to ensure the “rapid deployment” of forces and military capabilities in Saudi Arabia. Pakistan approved the agreement last week, whileTurkey's parliament began ratifying it [USN:L6N4660OA TEXT:"last week"]. Top officials from the three Mecca pact countries were meeting Iranian leaders in Tehran on Monday in [USN:L2N46C041 TEXT:"a push to de-escalate the conflict"]. Britain said [USN:SPN46200R TEXT:"last week"] it would deploy Royal Air Force Typhoon fighter jets on missions to help protect Saudi cities and critical infrastructure from Houthi aerial attacks. SISI SPELLS OUT LIMITS OF EGYPTIAN SUPPORT FOR SAUDIS The Cairo parliament had postponed the vote last week as Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty and intelligence chief Hassan Rashad travelled to Riyadh to deliver a letter to Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman from Sisi, who said Egypt's support would be limited to defending Saudi territory and borders rather than attacking Yemen. Abdelatty said afterwards that Cairo advocated exploring [USN:L1N4680Z9 TEXT:""every opportunity""] to resolve the Yemen conflict diplomatically. Essam Farid, the speaker of the Senate, said Egypt’s position was "purely defensive" and aimed at defending Saudi territory, borders, sovereignty and holy sites against external attack. He said that it would not extend to an attack on Yemen and that Egypt stands with its brothers as "a shield that protects, not a sword that attacks". Egypt, the Arab world's most populous state with one of the region's largest militaries, joined the Saudi-led coalition in an earlier phase of Yemen's war, in March 2015. At that time it acted mainly as a naval partner, sending warships to secure Red Sea shipping lanes. It also deployed around 800 ground troops but played only a limited combat role. Egypt was involved in a costly military intervention in Yemen in the 1960s and has not undertaken a large-scale foreign ground deployment since the 1991 Gulf War. Yahya Ali al-Rai, speaker of Yemen's Houthi-run House of Representatives, last week urged the Cairo parliament to reject the proposal, saying Egypt would be threatening its own national security and internal stability. The Senate speaker told the chamber he had received a letter from Ahmed Obeid bin Daghr, head of Yemen’s Shura Council, which is aligned with the internationally recognised government, backing Egypt’s participation in defending Saudi Arabia. Bin Daghr said the position reflected the will of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council, according to the speaker. Saudi Arabia is a major political and financial partner of Cairo, providing billions of dollars in aid, deposits at the central bank and energy supplies under Sisi. Fighting between the Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen's internationally recognised government and the Houthi militia, which controls the capital Sanaa, has escalated in recent weeks, becoming a volatile front in the US-Israeli war on Iran . The Houthis have attacked [USN:L1N45W03M TEXT:"Riyadh's international airport"] and the state oil company [USN:L1N45Z0HH TEXT:"Saudi Aramco"], disrupting flights and oil exports, while aid agencies have warned of worsening conditions in Yemen, already suffering one of the world's worst humanitarian crises. The Saudi crown prince had sought military help from the US, but President Donald Trump did not agree to strikes on the Houthis, people familiar with the matter told Reuters in September. Washington told Riyadh that it would help with intelligence sharing and targeting, they added. (This story has been corrected to change the attribution of the remarks to Sisi, not the letter, in paragraph 13.)

item.title: Netanyahu touts Trump endorsement on eve of vote, suggests they may restart war on Iran
item.description: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu boasted of his endorsement from Donald Trump on the eve of Israel's election, suggesting the two leaders could restart their war against Iran if he wins.
item.dc:creator: Steven Scheer, Emily Rose
item.content:encoded: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu boasted of his endorsement from Donald Trump on the eve of Israel's election, suggesting the two leaders could restart their war against Iran if he wins, after Trump said they should "finish the job". "US President Donald Trump has come with a friendship that has never existed before between an Israeli prime minister and an American president. And it is doubtful we will ever have such a friendly president again," Netanyahu said in a televised appearance late on Sunday night. "He has another two years, and he says he is calling on you to vote for me." In his own social media post on Sunday, Trump, who launched the Iran war jointly with Netanyahu in February, said: "Vote for Bibi Netanyahu for Prime Minister, we have to finish the job that we started!" Netanyahu said Trump was willing to take action "that would finally, finally, remove the Iranian threat", but only as long as Netanyahu himself remains in power. "And I have already instructed the Mossad and the IDF (military) to bring down this regime, to bring down this regime because that is the only way to put an end to this threat," Netanyahu said, referring to Israel's main intelligence service and military. Asked for comment on Netanyahu's remarks, White House Deputy Press Secretary Anna Kelly said: “As President Trump stated, Iran is in very bad condition, both economically and militarily, and the blockade will remain in full force and effect, with oil flowing in record numbers of barrels through the Hormuz Strait." "The United States will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the [TOPIC:"reuters:/world/us/elections/" TEXT:"midterm elections"]," Kelly added via email, referring to the November 3 vote in the US. Trump first endorsed Netanyahu on October 18, reiterating his support in a post on Truth Social on Sunday. Asked by reporters later on Monday whether Netanyahu had requested the second endorsement, Trump said: "I never spoke about it." "I put out both endorsements. I put out both... I think he's done a very good job as prime minister under very trying conditions." Netanyahu's leading opponent, centrist former military Chief of Staff Gadi Eisenkot, posted his own comments on social media, praising Trump as "a true friend of Israel". "I value his efforts and his commitment to Israel’s security, and I am confident that he will work in full cooperation with any leader chosen by the people." EISENKOT ACCUSES NETANYAHU OF FEAR-MONGERING Tuesday's vote, Israel's first since the October 7, 2023, Hamas attacks, is the first chance for voters to deliver a [USN:L8N4680E4 TEXT:"verdict on the worst security failure"] in generations and the wars on multiple fronts that followed. With Netanyahu already at the helm of the most right-wing government in Israeli history, politics have shifted even further to the right. Nearly all Jewish-led parties, including that of the hawkish Eisenkot, now [USN:L6N4660BW TEXT:"oppose the "two-state solution" that underpinned decades of peace negotiations"] with the Palestinians. But many voters say the divisive politics of Israel's longest-serving leader make the country weaker. Polls suggest Netanyahu's Likud Party will lose seats, potentially depriving his coalition of right-wing, far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties of its narrow majority. Eisenkot and an array of opposition parties ranging from the rump of the centre-left to the right, also have no clear path to unseat him. Netanyahu, 77, is an unrivaled master of political survival: the only time since 2009 that opponents managed to wrest him briefly from the premiership, it took four inconclusive elections within two years to get him out. He was back 18 months later. Neither side planned major public events for Monday. But both posted on social media, drumming on the election's major themes — for Netanyahu, that he is the only leader with the mettle to face down Israel's enemies; for his opponents, that his divisive politics have weakened the country. Netanyahu shared an AI-generated video on Monday of Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, whose father Ali Khamenei was killed on the first night of US-Israeli strikes on Iran in February. Lying in a hospital bed, the younger Khamenei says his own vote would be "definitely not Bibi. Another term like this and I will be meeting my father sooner than expected." On Sunday Netanyahu posted a computer-generated photo of a mushroom cloud over Tel Aviv, saying Israel was in existential danger from Iran. [USN:L6N46303T TEXT:"Eisenkot responded"] by accusing him of "relying on a campaign of fear-mongering, lies, and threats—including images of nuclear bombs in the heart of Tel Aviv. This time, it won’t work for him." Trump's endorsement of Netanyahu carries its own political risks a week before a legislative election in which his own Republicans are seeking to hold onto power. The Iran war is deeply unpopular in the United States, blamed for a surge in prices especially for fuel. Major fighting has been suspended for months after ceasefire negotiations held without Israeli participation.

item.title: Anthropic's soaring sales, steep losses put AI frenzy to IPO test
item.description: Anthropic took a big step closer to a potentially record-breaking IPO on Monday, even as it revealed steep losses and security concerns that could test investors' enthusiasm for the AI heavyweight.
item.dc:creator: Manya Saini, Echo Wang
item.content:encoded: Anthropic took a big step closer to a potentially record-breaking IPO on Monday, even as it revealed steep losses and security concerns that could test investors' enthusiasm for the AI heavyweight. AI has captured investors' imagination with the promise of a technological leap that could transform businesses, accelerate scientific breakthroughs and unlock vast productivity gains. That has fueled enormous investments in computing infrastructure and AI development, while also stoking skepticism over the scale and pace of the spending. Anthropic's listing comes at a critical time for global markets as investors closely assess whether the billions of dollars being poured into the technology will generate returns to justify sky-high valuations. "There is still enormous excitement about AI's potential to transform businesses, turbocharge productivity and reshape entire industries, but investors are becoming more discerning," said Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club. Anthropic's net loss in the first half of 2026 [USN:L4N4661JI TEXT:"widened sharply"] to $80.7 billion, largely due to a non-operating item related to bonds convertible into the company's shares. Despite the huge expenses, its operating loss for the same period narrowed to $693 million and its adjusted operating income swung to a positive $1.62 billion compared with a loss of $1.85 billion a year ago. The company, which is expected to go public before Thanksgiving, said its revenue grew a staggering 1,368% in the three months ended June 30 from a year ago, but it warned in the prospectus that its revenue growth rate could decline and fluctuate from time to time. The filing [USN:L4N4500J8 TEXT:"confirmed a series of Reuters "][USN:L4N4500J8 TEXT:"exclusives"] that offered an early peek at its contents before Anthropic made it public, including details of its financial performance, growth trajectory and IPO plans. Its prospectus details the risks from the powerful technology, from potential misuse and security threats to concerns that advanced systems could produce outputs that "could be interpreted as coercive, deceptive, or manipulative", including behavior resembling blackmail. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei [USN:L1N45403P TEXT:"has called for a slowdown"] in the development of AI. VALUATION EXPECTATIONS Some current and prospective investors [USN:L6N4611F6 TEXT:"are valuing Anthropic"] at about $1.5 trillion, down from roughly $2 trillion a week ago, after the AI startup disclosed some financial details at a [USN:L6N4601DE TEXT:"recent investor event"]. "The offering is for the faithful, that sooner or later, they're going to get some return on that invested capital," said Thomas Hayes, chairman at Great Hill Capital. Anthropic's IPO [USN:L6N46216E TEXT:"currently stands alone"] in what was once expected to be a crowded fall listing market. Analysts [USN:L6N46C0UF TEXT:"said"] that would give it access to a deep pool of capital to fund its costly AI ambitions. "Anthropic's IPO will establish a benchmark for valuing leading AI labs, influencing both upcoming listings and confidence in the companies funding the AI infrastructure build-out," IPOX research associate Lukas Muehlbauer said. Analysts expect valuations of the AI sector to correct as [USN:L6N4611C1 TEXT:"investor unease"] with the debt-fueled AI investment boom roils equity and debt markets. Higher borrowing costs and rising bond yields have also added to investor caution. "Anthropic is entering an IPO market that is far more challenging than the summer. Investors were not questioning valuations the same way a few months ago," said Matt Kennedy, senior strategist at Renaissance Capital, a provider of IPO-focused research and ETFs. BALANCING AI'S PROMISES AND PERILS Anthropic said more than half of Fortune 500 companies and over 30% of Global 2000 firms were its customers that generated at least $100,000 each in revenue for the company over the 12 months ended September 30. The IPO comes as Anthropic's own research raises concerns about advanced AI systems, which in controlled tests have shown behaviors including code sabotage, fraud assistance and information manipulation. "Our increasing use of AI systems to accelerate our own research and development may cause the capabilities of our models to advance more rapidly than our ability to develop, validate, and implement corresponding safety, alignment, and security measures," the prospectus said. The company said it relies on a limited number of cloud services providers such as Amazon, Google and Microsoft and suppliers such as Broadcom for compute and critical infrastructure parts. These relationships can create "dependencies and potential vulnerabilities", it said. Anthropic, which [USN:L4N41X0QE TEXT:"did not reveal"] the terms of its offering, will trade on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol "ANT" after the [USN:L4N469189 TEXT:"IPO closes"]. SCORCHING PACE OF GROWTH Anthropic, founded in 2021 by a team of researchers who left OpenAI after disagreements over governance and AI safety, was [USN:L4N4251UW TEXT:"valued at $965 billion"] in a funding round in May. It remains locked in a fierce battle with OpenAI to lead the race to build the most advanced AI systems. The company named Netflix's billionaire co-founder Reed Hastings as its lead independent director. In keeping with Nasdaq rules, Anthropic identified itself as a "controlled company" based on the power of its Long-Term Benefit Trust to elect a majority of its board. The company said it expects compute and infrastructure expenses to rise in absolute dollars and remain its largest operating expense. Anthropic has committed more than $600 billion to computing deals with partners including Amazon and Google, ranking among the largest AI infrastructure commitments on record. Anthropic's IPO follows that of Elon Musk's SpaceX, which rewrote the IPO record books in June, when it [USN:L6N42G18Z TEXT:"priced"] a $75 billion offering that valued the company at $1.75 trillion. Goldman Sachs secured the prestigious lead-left role on Anthropic's IPO, working alongside Morgan Stanley, which is also a lead underwriter. Both banks declined to comment. Twenty other banks were named as underwriters with Morgan Stanley serving as stabilization agent, overseeing the stock's early trading. The IPO mandates mark another win for the two banks, which also held lead roles in SpaceX's IPO.

item.title: AI gloom revives the specter of stagflation
item.description: AI skittishness has put the brakes on Wall Street's rally, resuscitating demand for US Treasuries as investors seek to protect portfolios, even as surging energy prices stoke inflation. This could put the Federal Reserve in an unenviable stagflationary bind.
item.dc:creator: Jamie McGeever
item.content:encoded: AI skittishness has put the brakes on Wall Street's rally, resuscitating [USN:L4N46803Y TEXT:"demand for US Treasuries"] as investors seek to protect portfolios, even as surging energy prices stoke inflation. This could put the Federal Reserve in an unenviable stagflationary bind. For most of this year, the US bond market has been slammed by an inflation-inducing barrage of soaring energy prices, fiscal fears, and the AI boom. Two of those forces remain very much in play, yet bond yields are no longer on a one-way path higher, with the 10-year falling below 5% for the first time in over a month last Thursday. Investor sentiment around AI is souring. While there has been no single obvious trigger, long-held concerns about the vast sums being spent on the technology have been exacerbated by Big Tech earnings reports detailing gargantuan capital expenditure plans. AI debt markets are wobbling too. While this all may prove to be temporary – just another speed bump in the AI race – the mood shift suggests we may be at the point in the cycle where almost any news is bad news. If so, this should spur a rally in “risk-free” Treasuries. If the AI juggernaut is sputtering, Wall Street and Main Street should sputter too, given how fundamental the technology has become to the stock market and economic growth. But the alarming fiscal outlook hasn't changed, and energy prices are roaring higher again, with US crude futures rising 10% last week to a six-month peak above $110 a barrel, suggesting price pressures and inflation expectations aren't cooling anytime soon. PERSISTENT PRICE PRESSURES A glance at a chart of the 10-year Treasury yield shows how closely correlated energy prices and the bond market have been this year. The 10-year yield's lowest daily close in 2026 was 3.96% on Friday, February 27, the day before the US and Israel attacked Iran. The subsequent surge in global crude, gas and fuel prices then propelled Treasury yields to their highest levels in more than two decades as investors bet that inflationary pressures would intensify. The 10-year yield reached 5.36% earlier this month. But that relationship has broken down recently. Oil prices eased for a few weeks beginning in mid-September, but the relentless rise in bond yields continued. Now oil prices have rebounded sharply, yet Treasury yields are in retreat, culminating in last Thursday's steep decline of 20 basis points. Typically, a global energy shock would be expected to slow economic growth, causing investors to flee to the Treasury market. However, for most of this year, the tailwind from the AI juggernaut has kept the economy and Wall Street humming. If the AI narrative is turning, bond investors will have to consider the potential valuation destruction and economic fallout from a deflating AI bubble. That appears to be offsetting any fears of "higher-for-longer" energy prices. But the move back toward Treasuries may not be a simple switch to flick. 'STAGFLATION' RETURN? That’s because "stagflation" could return to investors' lexicon. A mix of stagnant growth and sticky inflation would complicate life for the Federal Open Market Committee. While it raised its policy rate in September, it will almost certainly keep it on hold this Wednesday ahead of next week's midterm elections. Markets still expect it to tighten again in the coming months, but that assumes inflationary pressures outweigh AI wobbles. Last week, one-year market-based inflation expectations climbed to 2.80%, as measured by inflation swaps. That’s the highest since June, though the rise in longer-dated inflation swap rates has been less dramatic, suggesting investors don't believe the energy shock will become deeply embedded in higher goods and services prices. Fed policymakers will likely be banking on that. But it's a risky bet. Producer prices, often a leading indicator of consumer prices, are rising at the fastest pace in four years. The gap between producer and consumer price inflation is also the widest in four years. And it's worth repeating that consumer price inflation has been above the Fed's 2% target for close to six years. "All main inflation measures are expected to increase over the next couple of months as base effects from last year's government shutdown in October and November create a low bar for rising inflation," UBS economists say. "We expect little easing in inflation before the spring of next year," when the base effects from the start of the Iran war kick in. Can the Fed afford to "look through" the latest spike in energy prices, while hoping that the AI wobbles don't snowball?
