item.title: Serbia's new leaders face host of tough challenges
item.description: Serbia's student-led protest movement won a historic victory in Sunday's parliamentary election, ending the long rule of Aleksandar Vucic and sparking mass celebrations. But their yet-to-be named leaders face a long list of issues.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Serbia's student-led protest movement [USN:L6N46B017 TEXT:"won a historic victory"] in Sunday's parliamentary election, ending the long rule of Aleksandar Vucic and sparking mass celebrations. But their yet-to-be named [USN:L8N4650K6 TEXT:"leaders"] face a long list of issues. Here are a few of them: KOSOVO The Student List believes that Kosovo, which declared independence from Belgrade in 2008, remains an integral part of Serbia. During their campaign, the students' candidates said that Kosovo is a temporarily occupied territory which could be reintegrated into Serbia through peaceful means, diplomacy and dialogue. Their focus is preventing the exodus of the Serbian population in the north of Kosovo, and strengthening institutions funded by Serbia and operating under the Serbian legal system, such as healthcare and education. They want Kosovo's Serb communities to operate autonomously, rejecting previous agreements with the ethnic Albanian-led government in Pristina, such as those on energy, vehicle licence plates and the use of the dinar currency. FRAYED EU RELATIONS With Serbia's European Union accession talks largely stalled by a lack of necessary reforms, the Student List campaign deliberately avoided such polarising foreign policy issues. Prominent candidates, including former central bank governor Dejan Soskic and cardiologist Ilija Srdanovic, have said the government must first focus on domestic reforms and close all EU negotiating clusters before asking the public to cast a definitive ballot on membership of the bloc. The Student List position on Kosovo is also at odds with membership of the EU, which requires Belgrade to normalise relations with Pristina. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the bloc [USN:L6N46B0AC TEXT:"stood ready to support reforms"] including on the rule of law and media freedom, and to work together to advance Serbia’s future in the EU. COMPLEX RUSSIAN RELATIONSHIP AND US SANCTIONS AGAINST NIS OIL FIRM The Student List must navigate an intricate energy and foreign policy web with traditional Serbian ally Russia. The students have said they have no plans to align with the EU and impose sanctions on Moscow over its war in Ukraine. The new government would be reliant on US sanctions waivers to maintain crude imports while it waits for the [USN:L1N45M0TB TEXT:"sale of Russia's stake"] in energy company NIS (NIIS.BEL) , which operates Serbia's only oil refinery, to Hungary’s MOL (MOLB.BU) . Russia's Gazprom (GAZP.MM) is also Serbia’s biggest gas supplier, delivering around 2.2 billion cubic meters a year at below-market pricing. The Student List said this energy reliance was not a geopolitical alignment, but an acute economic dependency. The Student List's top candidates had not said whether a future government would end all arms exports from Serbia to war zones, including sales to Western intermediaries who pass weapons to Ukraine. Vucic cultivated strong personal ties with both Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy and Russian President Vladimir Putin. CORRUPTION The Student List’s anti-corruption program centres on institutional overhauls, such as the creation of an independent police unit accountable to prosecutors rather than the Interior Ministry and a purge of police officers linked to organised crime or violent crackdowns on protests. They want a ban on the appointments of party loyalists to state-owned companies in favour of transparent, merit-based hiring. Financial accountability and fiscal oversight would include a strict asset origin law allowing the state to audit, seize and return illegally acquired wealth from officials to the state budget. Convicted officials would be barred from holding public office. The students' anti-corruption program also envisions public scrutiny of all major state infrastructure contracts and the creation of independent oversight bodies to curb the misuse of public funds. Vucic, the SNS and the authorities repeatedly denied accusations of repression and corruption. ECONOMY Serbia's economy is deeply integrated with both the European market and international investment flows. The IMF has forecast Serbia's economic growth at 3% in 2026 and 4% in 2027. Inflation in September stood at 4.1%, almost double August's 2.2%, while the central bank has maintained a 5.75% benchmark rate since 2024. The Student List’s economic platform shifts Serbia’s growth model away from state-backed infrastructure projects and cheap labour to domestic market security and labour rights. Central to the plan is a campaign against retail monopolies to lower food prices, coupled with a tax overhaul that raises levies on wealthy citizens and cuts them for lower-income groups. The movement has pledged to sharply lower the maximum allowed duration for temporary work. Fiscal sustainability would rely heavily on anti-corruption savings and rigorous state oversight. Social spending would be focused on curbing a youth exodus through an affordable housing initiative for young couples, teachers and healthcare staff, alongside guaranteeing free school textbooks and cheaper, state-subsidised medication. (This story has been corrected to say top student leaders had not said whether a future government would halt weapons exports, in paragraph 15.)

item.title: In China, the AI bubble has already burst
item.description: While global tech stocks teeter, in China they have already crashed as lofty valuations collapse under worries about AI demand and curbs on Chinese exports.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: While global tech stocks teeter, in China they have already crashed as lofty valuations collapse under worries about AI demand and curbs on Chinese exports. The meltdown, tanking the mainland STAR50 index (.STAR50) of AI and semiconductor leaders by 40% in less than four months and vaporising some $480 billion in market value, is an ill omen for wobbly world markets and a dampener on China's efforts at encouraging its savers into stocks to fund the AI boom. It has also slammed the brakes on a rally running two years, since economic stimulus promises sent shares soaring, and has stalled Beijing's push to break with a long boom-bust pattern and drive a "slow bull" market that delivers reliable performance. China's broad blue-chip index (.CSI300) has dropped about 20% from highs made in June. "The stock market later evolved into a speculative crazy bull," said Beijing-based fund manager Dong Baozhen. "And now we see the bubble bursting." The reversal reflects a rally that ran to higher heights than markets in the West or elsewhere in Asia, and compares with a mere prick to US AI stocks, which have led a 6% drawdown in the Nasdaq (.IXIC) from a record high scaled three weeks ago. There has been no obvious selling trigger in China, although traders said high prices, tax bills and the threat of the US or other nations banning Chinese equipment in data centres all contributed. With AI stocks running to 42% of China's market capitalisation and 57% of turnover across mainland-listed A-shares and Hong Kong's H-shares, according to Goldman Sachs, few in a market dominated by small investors have escaped pain. RETAIL FAVOURITES SLIDE Shares in robot-maker Unitree (688836.SS) , 8,000 times oversubscribed by retail buyers at listing, have halved since they started trading in August, and chipmaker CXMT (688825.SS) has lost more than a quarter of its value in the past month. Chipmakers MetaX Integrated Circuits (688802.SS) and Moore Threads Technology (688795.SS) , which leapt 700% and 400% respectively on their market debuts last year, have also halved in value since July. Chen Wensheng, a small business owner and investor from China's southern Hainan, said he bought into the rally emboldened by what he felt was official support for the likes of Unitree, which counted state-backed funds as investors. But Chen and his friends are now nursing losses. Frustration that an investment theme backed by Beijing has ended so badly has driven many investors into defensive assets and is likely to slow equity fundraising by tech firms. Shares in optical parts makers Zhongji Innolight (300308.SZ) and Eoptolink Technology (300502.SZ) are down roughly 60% from highs in June and July, in part as Washington moves towards banning the one-time darlings from supplying US data centres. With the STAR50 index still at around 100 times trailing earnings, albeit down from a high of nearly 250, investors compare the Nasdaq 100's multiple of 30 and worry the selloff could get worse before it gets better. "What's happening is now going to put a stop for many of the companies trying to get themselves listed," said Hong Hao, managing partner and chief investment officer at Lotus Asset Management in Hong Kong. 'ALL BUBBLES INEVITABLY BURST' The frenzy and its [USN:L4N3YY09D TEXT:"fallout"] contrast with a push by authorities to improve returns and dampen volatility by cracking down on leverage and high-frequency trading. State-backed investors were sellers into rallies to keep gains in check. China's market regulator, the China Securities Regulatory Commission, did not immediately reply to questions faxed by Reuters last week. CRSC Chairman Wu Qing met with market participants earlier this month to hear suggestions on improving capital markets, the regulator said on its website, and some in the investment community say the boom has been bad for the market's structure. "Overemphasising the 'technology content' — that is, the weighting of tech companies by market value in major indexes — leads to a deviation, even a distortion, in capital behaviour," said Leo Wang, partner at Beijing-based Qianchuang Capital. "This created a severe bubble in certain sectors and a serious drain on others." Some see value in the selloff, saying it is neither surprising nor detrimental to market reforms that are geared for the long term and have gained traction in driving up returns, particularly income, in recent years. Although they have been sellers over the past three months, Asia funds in general are overweight on China, according to HSBC research. Goldman Sachs has Innolight and CXMT among dozens of Chinese AI stocks on a revamped recommendation list it published earlier this month, and BNP Paribas Securities strategist William Bratton has said the market offers buying opportunities for the careful. Still, on the mainland many are looking at other sectors or for even lower valuations before they turn buyers. "Just like all other Chinese manufacturers, (chipmakers and AI suppliers) will eventually end up in a price war," said fund manager Wang Zhuo, partner at Shanghai Zhuozhu Investment Management. "There's no exception," he said. "All bubbles inevitably burst."

item.title: Ambani, Adani outlets among Indian publishers contesting Modi’s privacy law
item.description: A group of 21 news publishers, including companies owned by billionaires Mukesh Ambani and Gautam Adani, has challenged India's privacy law in court, arguing it would trample investigative work and let New Delhi identify journalists' sources, documents show.
item.dc:creator: Aditya Kalra
item.content:encoded: A group of 21 news publishers, including companies owned by billionaires Mukesh Ambani and Gautam Adani, has challenged India's privacy law in court, arguing it would trample investigative work and let New Delhi identify journalists' sources, documents show. Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government last year announced implementation of a privacy law to [USN:L4N3WQ0V8 TEXT:"protect digital personal data"] of users, raising compliance requirements for platforms like Meta and Google. The publishers have said that since media outlets were not exempt, the law was an invasion of press freedom. Media companies received assurances in an August meeting with the government that the law would protect press freedom, but not having a written carve-out for journalists like in the European Union, Singapore and Britain was alarming, India's Digital News Publishers Association (DNPA) said in a confidential filing at the Supreme Court, reviewed by Reuters. The October 6 lawsuit, being reported for the first time and due to be heard on Tuesday, is the most high-profile challenge to Modi’s privacy law. Until now, only free speech activists and a group of smaller news outlets had [USN:L4N3ZZ10J TEXT:"challenged"] it. It also marks an unusual challenge to the government from businesses headed by Ambani and Adani, who opposition parties allege are close to Modi and get favourable treatment - charges the businesses and the government vehemently deny. DNPA and the media groups did not respond to requests for comment from Reuters, and neither did India's information technology ministry. The publishers are demanding that most of the law's contentious provisions, which kick in from May 2027, should be quashed. They are arguing the law could force a journalist to get prior consent from a person they want to investigate and force publishers to erase stories. They also say powers granted by the law to demand information could expose reporters' sources. The law would "render investigative journalism a benign and neutered recorder of events," the 698-page filing said. The provisions "constitute pre-censorship which is anathema to any democracy worth its name". The lawsuit comes amid accusations of declining press freedom in India since Modi took office in 2014. Critics say many mainstream media outlets have [USN:L4N43Q0BR TEXT:"not done enough"] to scrutinise Modi’s government. India's ranking in Reporters Without Borders’ World Press Freedom Index fell to 157th out of 180 countries this year, from 140th in 2014 - but the government rejects the rankings. Modi's government says it respects press freedom and says India, which has a "vibrant press and media ecosystem" of hundreds of newspapers and TV channels, does not need validation from foreign bodies. CONCERNS OVER CONSENT DNPA's members include Ambani's Network18, which has seven digital news platforms, Adani's NDTV (NDTV.NS) and other marquee media groups including the Indian Express and Times Internet, which is part of the Times of India group, publisher of India's largest-selling English-language daily. A key concern in the law is the requirement of consent, the group's filing says. A social media platform or online retailer can seek consent from users when they sign up, but the DNPA has argued that requiring a journalist to notify the subject of an investigation and seek consent "would allow that subject to destroy evidence, intimidate witnesses". The law also lets people withdraw consent at any time and demand that their data be erased, without any public-interest safeguard, which DNPA says could force its members to unpublish or heavily redact a factual news report. FEAR OF SOURCES AT RISK News publishers are concerned that a federal authority created under the law can impose fines for non-compliance, and grants powers to New Delhi to block access to any information in the "interests of the general public", which would curtail press freedom, DNPA said. In an August letter to the government attached to the lawsuit, the group said India "has chosen to grant broad exemptions to the state, while failing to extend any corresponding protection to the press". No response was cited. From next year, the law will also let New Delhi order any organization handling personal data “to furnish such information as it may call for”, putting newsrooms at risk of having to divulge sources, the filing said. It can also deter whistleblowers from sharing information on corruption, corporate wrongdoing or electoral malpractice with reporters, the DNPA argued. The “nakedly unguided” provision must be quashed, the DNPA said, adding that the power “can extend to privileged communications in possession of a reporter or the informant.”

item.title: Equities end higher as Anthropic's IPO filing buoys AI stocks
item.description: US stocks closed higher on Monday, with the S&P 500 and Nasdaq coming off consecutive weekly declines, as Anthropic's IPO filing helped boost sentiment in AI-related stocks in a week filled with a host of market catalysts.
item.dc:creator: Chuck Mikolajczak, Shashwat Chauhan
item.content:encoded: US stocks closed higher on Monday, with the S&P 500 and Nasdaq coming off consecutive weekly declines, as Anthropic's IPO filing helped boost sentiment in AI-related stocks in a week filled with a host of market catalysts. [USN:L3N46C10M TEXT:"Anthropic disclosed"] steep losses and red-hot revenue growth in its filing for a US initial public offering, laying out its ambition to build AI systems capable of reshaping the global economy despite the high costs of developing the technology. The AI lab is pushing ahead with its listing plans even as a once-lively autumn IPO calendar has slowed, with recent market volatility prompting companies to delay offerings. Anthropic's filing comes as investors increasingly dissect the potential payoff from massive AI spending and at the start of an eventful week. On tap are the Federal Reserve's policy statement on Wednesday, readings on economic growth and inflation on Thursday and a slew of corporate earnings reports throughout the week. More than a third of S&P 500 companies are scheduled to report earnings this week, including hyperscalers Alphabet (GOOGL.O) , Microsoft (MSFT.O) and Amazon.com (AMZN.O) , whose results will be [USN:L6N45T17Q TEXT:"parsed for signs"] of whether the hefty AI investments are translating into growth. "Today's all about the Anthropic release, so we're back on a little bit of an optimistic tilt, I would say. But there's a lot in that release. It will be interesting to see how well things are received when they actually come to list," said JP Powers, chief investment officer at RWA Wealth Partners in Boston. "The risk is maybe a little bit of a whipsaw if things aren't all moving in the same direction. A little optimism today, but who knows what will happen from some of these other releases this week," he said. The Dow Jones Industrial Average (.DJI) rose 146.42 points, or 0.28%, to 52,361.58, the S&P 500 (.SPX) gained 53.09 points, or 0.70%, to 7,676.77 and the Nasdaq Composite (.IXIC) gained 214.04 points, or 0.83%, to 26,169.38. Semiconductor and chip-related companies, widely viewed as some of the biggest beneficiaries of the AI boom, helped fuel the gains. The broader Philadelphia chips index (.SOX) was up 2.8% on the day but is still down 12.2% on the month. Meta shares closed down 1.9% after the social media company said it [USN:L3N46C0RT TEXT:"plans to raise"] up to $95 billion in equity to fund its AI-related expansion of data centers, cloud computing power and other infrastructure. The AI trade has come under pressure this month amid concerns that debt-funded spending may become harder to justify in the face of climbing borrowing costs. The Anthropic filing helped buoy sentiment, however, as neocloud firms, including CoreWeave (CRWV.O) , erased earlier declines. Other AI-linked companies, including photonic product makers Lumentum (LITE.O) and Coherent (COHR.N) , were among the best-performing S&P 500 stocks. Lumentum and Coherent gained about 8% and 6%, respectively. The technology index (.SPLRCT) led gains among the 11 major S&P 500 sectors, climbing 1.5%. Megacap and growth stocks were also mostly higher. Tesla (TSLA.O) jumped 5.2% to close at its highest level in more than three months after Barclays upgraded its rating on the stock to "overweight" from "equal-weight." Markets are pricing in only a 12.7% chance of a rate hike from the Fed on Wednesday, according to CME FedWatch. But with inflation pressures showing no signs of abating, market [USN:L6N46518P TEXT:"participants do not believe"] the central bank will be on hold for long. Investors are also bracing for the November 3 midterm elections , which will decide control of the US Congress. Advancing issues outnumbered decliners by a 1.36-to-1 ratio on the New York Stock Exchange and by a 1.09-to-1 ratio on the Nasdaq. The S&P 500 posted seven new 52-week highs and seven new lows, while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 82 new highs and 349 new lows. Volume on US exchanges was 16.7 billion shares, compared with the 17.2 billion average for the full session over the last 20 trading days.

item.title: Trump says Brazil election looked 'rigged,' defeated Bolsonaro's party recognizes Lula win
item.description: "I didn't take sides, but it looked like another rigged election," Trump told reporters, without providing any evidence. "It looked very bad to me."
item.dc:creator: Oliver Griffin, Eduardo Simões
item.content:encoded: US President Donald Trump said on Monday that leftist incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's surprise win in [USN:L2N46B01X TEXT:"Brazil's presidential vote"] "looked like another rigged election," although the party of defeated right-winger Flavio Bolsonaro later acknowledged the result. The son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, Flavio Bolsonaro has refused to concede defeat in [USN:L2N46B01X TEXT:"Sunday's presidential election"], saying he would seek the annulment of Lula's victory after the Supreme Court extended voting by two hours. Later on Monday, however, Bolsonaro's Liberal Party said it [USN:S0N46906S TEXT:"acknowledged the runoff result"] in a statement signed by the party's head Valdemar Costa Neto. "We recognize the presidential election results," Costa Neto said. "But we believe the issues raised need to be properly clarified." Bolsonaro, who has not commented publicly since his party's statement, said earlier on Monday he would comply with a federal police order to hand over his passports following a visit to his father, who is under house arrest, and denied he was planning to flee Brazil. Trump did not endorse Bolsonaro ahead of the vote, although Reuters has reported that officials from his State Department [USN:L1N4650X8 TEXT:"led a campaign"] to return the Bolsonaros to power. "I didn't take sides, but it looked like another rigged election," Trump told reporters, without providing any evidence. "It looked very bad to me." Bolsonaro lost to Lula by over 4 million votes, a clear result that it will be challenging for him to overturn. Fewer than 35,000 votes, or some 0.03% of the total, were cast in the extra two hours of voting ordered by the Supreme Court, according to an analysis of electoral records by Insper professor Pedro Burgos. "I just think it had a very bad look, the election, the way it was tabulated," Trump said. "The extension given was very strange." Vice President Geraldo Alckmin later defended Brazil's electoral system, saying in a TV interview with Rede Vanguarda that Trump's remarks were "totally wrong" and "unfounded." Neither Trump nor Jair Bolsonaro accepted their election losses in 2020 and 2022, respectively. Brazil's former president was handed a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after losing to Lula. Analysts do not expect Flavio Bolsonaro to be able to build the same anti-democratic movement as his father in 2022. MARKETS ROILED BY LULA WIN World leaders have already widely congratulated Lula on his unprecedented fourth mandate, which was greeted with [USN:L2N46C051 TEXT:"dismay by investors"] who had been betting on a Bolsonaro win. Brazil's real fell 8.1% against the dollar in its biggest one-day drop since 2002, while the stock exchange marked its steepest one-day fall since 2020. "The initial selloff could moderate as election-related positions are unwound, but investors will demand convincing fiscal commitments before rebuilding exposure," said Pantheon Macroeconomics' chief Latin America economist Andres Abadia. Lula's victory defied polls, precedent and global anti-incumbent sentiment to put the brakes on a wave of right-wing election victories across Latin America. He trailed Bolsonaro in the first round, but managed to convince voters to come out for him in the runoff. Pollsters said a higher-than-expected turnout and an improved [USN:L6N46815Z TEXT:"social media campaign"] helped power Lula to victory. During the campaign, Lula pointed to his track record of cutting poverty and inequality while also highlighting record-low unemployment, illiteracy and deforestation, but his fourth term may prove challenging. He will face an [USN:L6N46B06R TEXT:"uphill battle"] for his agenda in a Congress [USN:L6N45R137 TEXT:"packed with Bolsonaro allies"] after a surge of conservative voters in the first round of the general election pushed the Brazilian legislature further to the right.

item.title: Houthis say they attacked Saudi oil pumping stations, Riyadh airport as fighting intensifies
item.description: The Iran-aligned group continued attacks as rising hostilities choke oil supplies and threaten to erupt into a larger conflict.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said on Monday they had attacked Saudi Arabia's East-West crude oil pumping stations and Riyadh airport, as rising hostilities choke oil supplies and threaten to erupt into a larger conflict. The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said earlier it had destroyed two ballistic missile launchers in the capital Sanaa, including one used to fire a missile towards Riyadh that the coalition said it had intercepted. There was no immediate Saudi confirmation of the Houthi attacks. The Houthis have been firing ballistic missiles and drones at Saudi airports, ports and oil installations, turning US ally Saudi Arabia into a pressure point in the wider war. The Houthis also said they had struck Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport, which [USN:L2N46A05D TEXT:"resumed operations at two terminals"] on Sunday after an attack claimed by the group [USN:L1N45W03M TEXT:"earlier this month"] killed 13 people, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade. Top officials from the Mecca Pact countries Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan are set to meet Iranian officials in Tehran on Monday to discuss regional coordination, two people with knowledge of the matter said. The planned talks would be the first high-level contact between Iran and all members of the three-nation bloc since Saudi Arabia came under escalating attacks from Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis. STRIKES INSIDE YEMEN Saudi Arabia [USN:L6N453173 TEXT:"temporarily shut down"] its 1,200-km (746-mile) East-West pipeline in September as a precaution after a drone attack that Riyadh and Baghdad said originated in Iraq. The pipeline has served as a key route for Middle East oil exports while the Strait of Hormuz has been largely shut by the war. The Houthis also said on Saturday they had targeted the East-West pipeline, crude oil pumping stations, an Aramco facility in Yanbu and the Rabigh refinery. There was no Saudi confirmation of those claims. The Saudi coalition said on Monday it had also carried out a military operation against Houthi targets in Yemen, destroying five tunnels used to store ballistic missiles, four ballistic missile launchers and a missile storage facility. The operation also targeted Houthi supply lines, fighters and military equipment along front lines inside Yemen, coalition spokesperson Turki al-Maliki said, pledging continued "deterrent operational measures" to protect civilians. Saudi Arabia has intensified its strikes on the Houthis since the group captured strategic areas along Yemen's Red Sea coast last month, advancing towards the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a key global shipping route for Gulf oil producers on the other side of the Arabian Peninsula from the Strait of Hormuz. The latest fighting has effectively ended a UN-brokered truce that had largely held since 2022. Saudi Arabia led a coalition into Yemen's civil war in 2015 to back the internationally recognised government, a year after the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa.

item.title: Jordan says its air force struck 'militant hideouts' in Syria after church attack
item.description: Jordan said on Monday its air force struck what it described as militant hideouts in southern Syria after determining that the suspects behind last week's deadly church attack in the kingdom were linked to "terrorist groups" operating there.
item.dc:creator: Abdelhadi Ramahi, Yasmine Ghania, Muhammad Gebaly
item.content:encoded: Jordan said on Monday its air force struck what it described as militant hideouts in southern Syria after determining that the suspects behind last week's deadly church attack in the kingdom were linked to "terrorist groups" operating there. The armed forces said the operation was conducted in coordination with Damascus. Syria's government gave a contradictory account, saying it had launched an investigation into the Jordanian attacks, and stressed in a statement the importance of field and security coordination in border areas. Damascus informed Jordan of its "complete reservation" over the strikes without prior coordination, the foreign ministry said in a statement. Seven people, including three children and a woman, were killed and three others were wounded in the Jordanian strikes, the Syrian Civil Defence said in a preliminary report. It said emergency teams responded to four sites hit by the strikes in the countryside of Daraa and Sweida provinces. There was no immediate comment from Jordan on that account. Shortly after the strikes, Syria closed the Nassib border crossing with Jordan on Tuesday, suspending passenger and commercial traffic in both directions, citing developments on the ground in Daraa province, the Syrian General Authority for Border Crossings and Customs said in a statement. Nassib is Jordan's only passenger and commercial border crossing with Syria. Earlier on Monday, senior government security officials said Jordanian security forces had arrested two brothers and their brother-in-law after a shootout on Monday over the church violence that killed nine people. "God willing, they only represent themselves," said Jordan's Director of Public Security, Major-General Obeidallah al-Maaytah. Such violence is rare in Jordan, a relatively stable US ally in the Middle East. Friday's attack on the Christian minority prompted King Abdullah to order security forces to respond with an "iron fist". In a press conference, al-Maaytah and Interior Minister Mazen al-Faraya said the country would not tolerate extremist terrorism. "The file has not yet been closed; investigations are still ongoing. As of today, there are no indications of any links between them and other cells," al-Faraya added. ATTACK TARGETED GREEK ORTHODOX FUNERAL Friday's assault during a funeral at a Greek Orthodox church in the village of Hamoud, about 120 km (75 miles) southwest of the capital, Amman, also wounded at least 34 people. [USN:L6N46B02Q TEXT:"Witnesses"] said gunmen opened fire for several minutes. The suspects, who lived near Hamoud, will face justice, said the security officials. The three suspects were named in the press briefing. Reuters video footage showed a building pockmarked by the exchange of fire in the village of al-Judayyda, in Karak governorate. Jordan's Public Security Directorate said in a statement carried by state media that security forces located the suspects while they were hiding in an abandoned house. They refused to surrender and attacked security forces, who returned fire and arrested all three after wounding them. No security personnel were injured, and security forces found a number of firearms and rounds of ammunition in the suspects' possession. There has been no claim of responsibility for the church attack. Jordan, a US partner in the fight against extremism, has foiled Islamist militant plots in the past. The security officials did not name any Islamist groups in the press conference.

item.title: Saudi defence pact countries push for peace in Tehran as Houthis launch more attacks
item.description: Top officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan met Iranian officials in Tehran on Monday in a bid to de-escalate the Middle East conflict, as Yemen's Houthis launched new attacks on Saudi Arabia and Egypt approved defence support for the Gulf kingdom.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Mills, Ariba Shahid, Menna Alaaeldin
item.content:encoded: Top officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan met Iranian officials in Tehran on Monday in a bid to de-escalate the Middle East conflict, as Yemen's Houthis [USN:L2N46C045 TEXT:"launched new attacks"] on Saudi Arabia and Egypt [USN:S8N44701K TEXT:"approved defence support"] for the Gulf kingdom. The talks were the first high-level contact between Iran and the three nations — which signed the Mecca mutual defence pact in August — since a war that began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran also spread to Saudi Arabia and Yemen. Saudi Arabia said the visit was intended to open negotiating channels to "prevent the return of military escalation". It was represented by Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, younger brother of Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman; Pakistan by army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir; and Turkey by intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin, Saudi and Iranian officials said. Iranian state media published pictures of Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi and Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, attending the meetings. At the conclusion, the four states agreed to continue talks with a view to strengthening cooperation in peace and security, state media reported. Pakistan and Qatar have led mediation efforts in the war. Earlier efforts helped produce an [USN:L6N42N0OL TEXT:"interim peace agreement"] in June, but fighting between Iran and the US soon resumed. Conflict then flared between the Iran-aligned Houthis and US ally Saudi Arabia, opening a new front. US AND IRAN THREATEN NEW ATTACKS The wider fighting has restricted shipping through the energy chokepoint of the [USN:L8N3YO10W TEXT:"Strait of Hormuz"], pushed up [USN:L2N46B09G TEXT:"global oil and gas prices"], left Gulf states facing missile and drone attacks, and caused a new [USN:L6N46C0OE TEXT:"humanitarian crisis"] in Yemen. Tensions between Washington and Tehran have sharpened recently, with President Donald Trump [USN:L1N469125 TEXT:"saying on Friday"] the US may strike Iran again. Iranian security officials told Reuters Tehran had [USN:L6N46816Q TEXT:"drawn up detailed plans"] to attack Gulf undersea cables if the US and Israel attack again. The war, which earlier in the year also reignited fighting between Israel and the Iran-backed Lebanese Hezbollah militia, has eroded Trump's approval ratings ahead of the US [USN:L6N46017L TEXT:"midterm elections"] that decide control of Congress. Iranian security chief Rezaei said the visit by the three countries had shown that "American threats have little impact on countries around the world". He spoke of a "new and positive atmosphere" in the region. Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei had earlier said the meeting, proposed when Munir visited Tehran [USN:L1N4660R4 TEXT:"last week"], could be a first step towards establishing regional security mechanisms. A senior Pakistani security official said the focus was on building a regional non-aggression network. The agenda also included US-Iran talks, Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, the Strait of Hormuz and a US blockade of Iranian ports, they said. Another Pakistani official said Munir, with a go-ahead from Trump to try diplomacy, had presented Iran with a solution to the conflict that would offer something to both the US and Iran, without giving details. The Mecca pact states and Qatar could act as guarantors if it was accepted, the official added. An Iranian official had earlier said there would be [USN:S8N42207J TEXT:"no discussion"] of Iran's [USN:L1N45T0JD TEXT:"nuclear programme"] at Monday's meeting, and the issue would not be addressed until Tehran's demands for ending the war were met. Those conditions include ending a US blockade of Iranian ports and lifting sanctions on Iranian oil exports. US Vice President JD Vance [USN:L1N45T0DK TEXT:"has said"] Iran must reduce nuclear enrichment to end the war. Pakistan's military media office and Turkey's Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment. PARLIAMENT APPROVES EGYPTIAN DEFENCE SUPPORT FOR SAUDIS Saudi Arabia has intensified strikes against the Houthis since they captured strategic areas along Yemen's Red Sea coast last month, advancing against Saudi-backed government forces. The Houthis have hit Saudi airports, ports and oil facilities. On Monday, the Houthis said they had attacked pumping stations on Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline as well as Riyadh airport, which said it had [USN:L2N46A05D TEXT:"resumed operations"] at two terminals a day earlier. There was no immediate Saudi confirmation of the Houthi attacks. Parliament in Egypt, which has said it is considering joining the Mecca pact, on Monday authorised the Egyptian military to help defend Saudi Arabia, a major financial and political partner for Cairo. The [USN:L6N4440IT TEXT:"Mecca Joint Defence Agreement"] says signatories shall use "all necessary means" to eliminate threats to one another's territorial integrity, sovereignty or internationally recognised borders, according to a text seen by Reuters. The pact's members held an emergency meeting in Riyadh this month and [USN:L1N45R0S7 TEXT:"agreed to ensure"] the "rapid deployment" of military forces and capabilities in Saudi Arabia. Efforts by Turkey’s parliament to ratify the agreement began last week and are still under way, while Pakistan approved the pact last week.

item.title: World stocks gain ahead of 'formidable' week for risk; oil prices fall
item.description: Global shares advanced on Monday, with investors focused on central bank meetings and a week of corporate earnings that will test confidence in the AI boom.
item.dc:creator: Chris Prentice, Amanda Cooper
item.content:encoded: Global shares advanced on Monday, with investors focused on central bank meetings and a week of corporate earnings that will test confidence in the AI boom. Oil prices retreated after Friday's strong gains, amid signs of easing hostilities in the Middle East. Still, prices remained near recent highs as persistent attacks on key producer Saudi Arabia kept traders wary. The Houthi group in Yemen said on Monday it had attacked Saudi Arabia's [USN:L2N46C045 TEXT:"East-West crude oil"] pumping stations and Riyadh airport. MSCI's gauge of stocks across the globe (.MIWD00000PUS) rose 4.22 points, or 0.38%, to 1,123.19. On Wall Street, major indexes climbed on tech strength after Anthropic's [USN:L3N46C10M TEXT:"initial public offering"] filing. The Dow Jones Industrial Average (.DJI) rose 146.42 points, or 0.28%, to 52,361.58, the S&P 500 (.SPX) gained 53.09 points, or 0.7%, to 7,676.77 and the Nasdaq Composite (.IXIC) gained 214.04 points, or 0.83%, to 26,169.38. Brazilian stocks posted historic losses. The country's stock exchange [USN:L6N46C031 TEXT:"halted trading"] via a circuit breaker safety mechanism on Monday after [USN:L6N4681ER TEXT:"President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's reelection"]. His opponent refused to concede. In Europe, stocks rebounded on corporate optimism. The STOXX 600 (.STOXX) closed up 0.77%, led by gains in British technology services provider Computacenter (CCC.L) and Danish biotech Genmab (GMAB.CO) . ALPHABET, MICROSOFT, AMAZON AMONG REPORTING COMPANIES Traders awaited multiple central bank meetings and earnings from AI hyperscalers. [USN:L6N46919T TEXT:"Earnings"] are in store from Alphabet (GOOGL.O) , Microsoft (MSFT.O) and Amazon (AMZN.O) , as one-third of S&P 500 companies report. "The combination is formidable: megacap earnings, AI funding concerns, global semiconductor results, five major central bank meetings and potentially market-moving inflation and growth data," said Chris Weston, Pepperstone's head of research. "The danger isn't simply that markets move sharply. It's that one catalyst changes the interpretation of the next, creating feedback loops across equities, rates, FX and volatility," Weston added. [USN:L4N4690C8 TEXT:"New Zealand's"] central bank is widely expected to raise rates on Wednesday. Markets assume the US [USN:L6N46606V TEXT:"Federal Reserve"] will stand pat, but they imply an 80% chance that it will hike rates in December. Much the same is priced in for the [USN:L4N4650KC TEXT:"Bank of Japan"] and the [USN:L6N45U0QU TEXT:"European Central Bank"]. , , A key reading on US core inflation should show cost pressures remained elevated at 3.1% in September, while the economy is forecast to have grown at a brisk 3.2% annualized pace thanks in part to spending on data centers. "The most important risk is that oil futures are above our forecasts, largely reflecting concerns about potential further conflict with Iran," analysts at Goldman Sachs said in a note. "The more extreme and long-lasting the energy shock becomes, the more Fed participants will worry that inflationary pressures could broaden." Emerging market stocks (.MSCIEF) fell 15.13 points, or 0.96%, to 1,562.91. MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan (.MISX00000PUS) closed 0.15% lower at 1,505.49. TREASURIES AND CURRENCIES The Brazilian real plunged after the presidential election. The yield on benchmark US 10-year notes was flat at 4.988%. The yield on the benchmark German 10-year Bund rose. In currency markets, the Japanese yen slipped 0.43%, and the euro was down 0.25% . The dollar index , which measures the greenback against a basket of currencies including the yen and the euro, rose 0.34%. Sterling dipped 0.24% , with Britain's new finance minister [USN:L1N46206Z TEXT:"John Healey"] set to deliver his first budget on Wednesday amid rising global borrowing costs and high energy prices due to the US-Israeli war with Iran. Spot gold rose 0.46% to $4,013.79 an ounce, rebounding from the prior session's more than three-month low. US gold futures settled 0.8% higher at $4,038.40 per ounce. Saudi Arabia, which along with Turkey and Pakistan was set to hold talks with Iranian officials in Tehran, said it was important to open channels for negotiations. On Sunday, Qatari mediators traveled to Tehran to try to de-escalate regional tensions in coordination with the United States, an official briefed on the situation said. Brent crude futures finished down 0.78% at $115.81 per barrel, as US crude settled down 1.46% at $101.76.

item.title: As weight-loss drug users turn to dietary supplements, doctors and regulators raise flags
item.description: For Allison Vecchio, 42, GLP-1 drugs were "a reset button on life," but at a price — side effects like gastrointestinal distress, brittle nails, and feelings of weakness so intense that at times she could not leave her bed.
item.dc:creator: Nicholas Brown
item.content:encoded: For Allison Vecchio, 42, GLP-1 drugs were "a reset button on life," but at a price — side effects like gastrointestinal distress, brittle nails, and feelings of weakness so intense that at times she could not leave her bed. This is the second story in a five-part Reuters series on how weight-loss drugs are changing the way people shop and eat, and how companies are responding to the trend But the Fort Pierce, Florida-based ER nurse said the symptoms eased when she began a cocktail of supplements that included fiber, collagen and electrolytes, a haul that costs $200 to $300 a month. "You really have to take the reins" to turn mere weight loss into improved health, she said. GLP-1 drugs like Novo Nordisk's (NOVOb.CO) Ozempic and Wegovy rank among the biggest medical breakthroughs in years, owing to their efficacy in treating obesity and type 2 diabetes, and reducing the risk of heart disease. Some 10 million Americans used them last year, a figure that could grow to 25 million by 2030, according to JPMorgan research. Their side effects, though, have caused many to turn to loosely regulated dietary supplements. US supplement sales have surged in recent years, surpassing $74 billion in 2025, according to the Nutrition Business Journal. While users swear by them, their growing popularity — fueled in part by social media — has doctors raising red flags and regulators considering new rules around how these products come to market. Vitamins and supplements don't need preapproval by the US Food and Drug Administration, making their scientific credibility hard to gauge. With social media personalities playing a growing role in their promotion, some medical researchers have called for more regulation of online supplement marketing. Rob Fried, CEO of Niagen Bioscience (NAGE.O) , which had $129 million in sales last year, cautioned that companies "can hire an influencer, or even hundreds of influencers on TikTok ... to make whatever claims will sell." SALES OF SUPPLEMENTS SOAR Vecchio has 25,000 TikTok followers and is on retainer with three brands. She is also a member of TikTok Shop's HealthPro creator program, which is reserved for licensed health professionals. Pittsburg, Kansas, resident Terri Hart, 52 — a TikToker with more than 12,000 followers — mostly works on commission, perusing products the brands make available to influencers, and promoting the ones she feels helped her the most. Hart takes magnesium, electrolytes, B12 and other supplements, which she says have helped offset what she called "horrible" nausea, fatigue and constipation after beginning GLP-1s in 2023. They run about $110 a month, costs insurance doesn't cover. TikTok income eases the burden, Hart says. She says she makes clear she isn't a medical professional, and urges followers to talk to doctors before taking her advice. "I establish my authority through my lived experience," Hart said. TikTok Shop generated more than $1 billion in dietary supplement sales in 2025, or 5.4% of all e-commerce supplement sales, according to the Nutrition Business Journal, while overall US vitamin and supplement sales grew 5% in 2024 and 7% last year. The drugs are "bringing in new consumers and expanding existing supplement routines," said Erika Craft, a data analyst at Nutrition Business Journal. But absent FDA preapproval, people don't know exactly what is in many supplements, said Jonathan Bonnet, a clinical associate professor at Stanford and chief medical officer at the Ardmore Institute of Health in Ardmore, Oklahoma. "If you can't know what you're taking, it's hard to know what risks you're undergoing," he said. RETAILERS OFFER MORE SUPPLEMENTS Nearly half of GLP-1 users started taking new vitamins and supplements after beginning the drugs, according to a Nutrition Business Journal survey, with probiotics, protein and fiber particularly popular. A consumer survey by Boston Consulting Group this year said GLP-1 users spend roughly 20% more on protein, fiber and collagen, a protein that helps maintain skin structure, than before starting the drugs. Companies are capitalizing. Target (TGT.N) is widening its supplement offerings, while private equity-owned The Vitamin Shoppe has seen double-digit sales growth this year in fiber and creatine, which are both popular with GLP-1 users, said Jack Gayton, senior vice president of merchandising at The Vitamin Shoppe. Mergers and acquisitions in the space are getting bigger, though with fewer transactions. In 2024, there were 115 deals globally worth $7.3 billion, according to financial data firm PitchBook. In 2025, there were 95 deals worth $16.9 billion. Through October 6 of this year, there have been 68 deals worth $14.6 billion. Procter & Gamble (PG.N) is [USN:L4N4411L4 TEXT:"set to acquire"] supplement maker Thorne, while Japan's Kirin Holdings announced in August it will buy Canada's Jamieson Wellness (JWEL.TO) , whose US-based brand youtheory released a product aimed at GLP-1 users in early 2025. Jamieson spokesperson Ruth Winker said the company sees GLP-1s as a tailwind for growth beyond combating side effects. "As people get healthier, they tend to take more vitamins and supplements," Winker said. REGULATIONS IN THE OFFING US Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has proposed tighter regulations. The FDA this year has stepped up efforts to strengthen oversight of new dietary ingredients, issuing new guidance on what submissions for review should include. Many supplement makers avoid this review process by using a pathway that allows food companies to declare ingredients “generally recognized as safe" without notifying the FDA. But a proposed rule would eliminate that option as part of Kennedy's broader effort to regulate food ingredients. The proposal has divided the industry. Some support more regulation, lamenting unscrupulous actors who spike supplements with drugs or add only tiny amounts of touted beneficial ingredients. “At a minimum, a review process should happen prior to launch," says Jacqueline Maslan, CEO of Body of Work, a vitamin startup aimed at women under 40. But supplement trade group the Council for Responsible Nutrition says the rule would cause months of backlogs as the FDA reviews thousands of ingredients. Thorne CEO Colin Watts said it's “improbable” the FDA could have the manpower to review new ingredients “at the speed needed to keep up with innovation." In a statement to Reuters, an HHS spokesperson said the FDA is mulling opportunities "to modernize its regulatory approach to keep pace with an evolving marketplace," adding the agency wants to ensure product safety "while supporting consumer choice." item.title: How one hacker used AI agents and a few thousand dollars to break into scores of sites
item.description: A report found AI agents attempted 1,200 break-ins and compromised more than 100 sites.
item.dc:creator: Raphael Satter
item.content:encoded: Over the past couple of weeks, a cybersecurity researcher watched as a Chinese-speaking hacker broke into websites belonging to more than 100 companies, including farm equipment maker Deere (DE.N) , home appliance company SharkNinja (SN.N) and engine manufacturer Cummins (CMI.N) . Yet the hacker did almost none of the work. The cybercriminal instead outsourced the hacking spree almost entirely to artificial intelligence, tasking AI agents with spending hours autonomously probing and breaking into targeted sites, according to Snorre Fagerland, principal threat researcher at the cybersecurity company NorForge. In a report provided to Reuters ahead of publication on Monday , Fagerland said the hacker was one of several he discovered while scanning the web for inadvertently exposed instances of Cairn, an open-source AI problem-solving platform popular with hackers. Beginning around October 2, Fagerland said he found about two dozen instances of Cairn being used for malicious activity, which allowed him to quietly peer over the cybercriminals' shoulders as they set their AI tools loose on the world. Fagerland's report on the Chinese-speaking hacker did not name the victims, but Reuters was able to establish the victims' identities by independently reviewing the hacker's Cairn activity. At a time of [USN:L4N456128 TEXT:"rising anxiety"] over the power of autonomous AI tools, Fagerland said his find was real-life evidence that commercially available AI agents could pull off complex intrusions from start to finish without human intervention, a dramatic boost to the power of a single malicious actor. "It's a new world now," said Fagerland. Reuters could not ascertain the degree to which the breaches resulted in unauthorized extraction of data. Deere told Reuters it had taken "necessary remediation actions" following the incident and had "no indication that sensitive information was accessed." SharkNinja said the hack had hit a standalone site carrying only product support information and that the threat had been contained. Cummins said it was "investigating the report of a potential cyber-attack on a website operated by one of our third-party vendors." Two smaller businesses also acknowledged being compromised. Other victims listed in the Cairn data did not return messages. FEW INSTRUCTIONS, MANY HACKS One of the hackers that Fagerland observed stole a trove of credit card data. Another tried to get AI agents to rob a cryptocurrency exchange. The Chinese-speaking hacker was the most prolific. Beginning on September 25, they set their AI army loose against US, Canadian, Australian and Japanese e-commerce websites. Their instructions were terse, sketching out their preferred intrusion tactics in fewer than 100 Chinese characters. As of late last week, their agents had attempted to break into more than 1,200 sites. Successful intrusions typically took around 23 hours of poking and prodding for vulnerabilities. Fagerland estimated that the campaign, which appeared to be using a mixture of China's DeepSeek and Anthropic's Claude Code, had chewed up roughly $5,000 worth of tokens, or about $50 per successful hack. Fagerland — who has worked in cybersecurity for nearly three decades — said he was impressed by some of the techniques the agents used to compromise their victims. In one case, after failing to find any weaknesses in a big company's public-facing application, the AI agents pored through digital records to find associated infrastructure, located a public-facing control panel, discovered a subtle weakness in the way it processed data, and after hours of trial and error, reported leveraging it to trick the server into executing malicious commands. "It's not straightforward to come up with solutions like that," Fagerland said. "It's not script kiddie stuff." Cairn's author, whose social media handle is "le1xia0", acknowledged receipt of a Reuters message but did not immediately answer a list of questions. In a recent post on X, they said their platform was "an innovative type of multi-agent architecture and was not designed for hacking attacks. If it is used to carry out harmful hacking attacks, that is not my intention." NO SUPERVISION NEEDED The ability of agentic AI systems to autonomously discover vulnerabilities, conduct intrusions, and steal data is a source of increasing anxiety around the world. Rogue agents inadvertently unleashed by major AI companies have [USN:L6N45H0LE TEXT:"hacked their way out of computer labs"][USN:L6N45H0LE TEXT:","] [USN:L4N45G0G8 TEXT:"broken into government websites"], and engaged in [USN:L6N44B0TQ TEXT:"unsanctioned social engineering attempts"]. South Korea and Japan have in recent weeks been buffeted by a series of well-publicized hacks attributed to [USN:L1N45U0IU TEXT:"AI-using cybercriminals"]. AI agents are increasingly becoming staples of the cybercriminal underground. In August, the Israeli firm Gambit Security found that Russian-speaking extortionists had [USN:L6N44N0S2 TEXT:"leveraged SpaceX's Cursor AI tool"] to break into seven organizations. In September, Gambit documented an AI agent-driven spree that resulted in breaches at 25 companies and the theft of at least 600,000 credit card records. Last week, the cyber intelligence company Bitsight said that discussions about how to use autonomous agents were surging across cybercriminal forums . Fagerland said he had previously assumed hacker-agents would need at least some supervision. He said it was now obvious that the technology had moved past that. "The development in this field is astounding," he said.

item.title: Anthropic's path from AI startup to industry-defining IPO
item.description: Anthropic on Monday unveiled its IPO filing, moving closer to what could be the first public listing by a frontier AI lab, outlining the technology's potential while also laying bare the risks and costs of developing it.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Anthropic on Monday [USN:L4N45L0EZ TEXT:"unveiled its IPO filing"], moving closer to what could be the first public listing by a frontier AI lab, outlining the technology's potential while also laying bare the risks and costs of developing it. Here is a look at the road to the planned IPO: May 2021: Anthropic, led by siblings Dario Amodei and Daniela Amodei, announces it has raised $124 million in a Series A funding round led by technology investor and Skype co-founder Jaan Tallinn. April 2022: Anthropic raises $580 million in a Series B funding round. March 2023: The company [USN:L1N35L3G1 TEXT:"releases"] a large language model, Claude, that competes directly with offerings from OpenAI. May 2023: Anthropic [USN:L4N37K23L TEXT:"raises $450 million"] from investors including Alphabet's (GOOGL.O) Google and Spark Capital. September 2023: Amazon.com (AMZN.O) [USN:L1N3AY2VF TEXT:"announces"] it will invest up to $4 billion in cash in Anthropic. October 2023: Alphabet's Google [USN:L4N3BX52Q TEXT:"agrees"] to invest up to $2 billion in Anthropic. March 2024: Anthropic [USN:L2N3FH0F3 TEXT:"reveals a suite of AI models"] known as Claude 3. The company says the most capable in the family, Claude 3 Opus, outperforms rival models GPT-4 from OpenAI and Gemini 1.0 Ultra from Google on various benchmarks. August 2024: Anthropic is [USN:L1N3K70J9 TEXT:"hit with a class-action lawsuit"] in California federal court by three authors who say it misused their books and hundreds of thousands of others to train its AI-powered chatbot Claude. November 2024: Amazon.com [USN:L4N3MT10T TEXT:"pumps"] another $4 billion into Anthropic. March 2025: Anthropic [USN:L3N3PF1EX TEXT:"raises $3.5 billion"] at a $61.5 billion post-money valuation led by Lightspeed Venture Partners. September 2025: Anthropic's [USN:L4N3UP19S TEXT:"valuation hits"] $183 billion post-money, after raising $13 billion in a new round. September 2025: Anthropic [USN:L6N3VG0H8 TEXT:"unveils"] the Claude 4.5 AI model, saying the newest version can code for longer uninterrupted stretches and handle finance and scientific tasks better. February 2026: The company [USN:L4N3Z827V TEXT:"raises $30 billion"] in a funding round, more than doubling the Claude chatbot maker's valuation to $380 billion. February 2026: U.S. President Donald Trump [USN:FWN3ZN2FT TEXT:"says"] he is directing the government to stop work with Anthropic, while the Pentagon said it would declare the startup a supply-chain risk. March 2026: Anthropic [USN:L6N3ZR1I4 TEXT:"files a lawsuit"] to block the Pentagon from placing it on a national security blacklist, escalating the AI lab's high-stakes battle with the U.S. military over usage restrictions on its technology. April 2026: Anthropic [USN:L4N40Q0LK TEXT:"debuts Mythos"], its most advanced AI model to date, equipped with sophisticated capabilities and designed for defensive cybersecurity tasks. May 2026: Anthropic announces it has [USN:L4N4251UW TEXT:"raised $65 billion"] at a post-money valuation of $965 billion. June 2026: Anthropic [USN:L4N4291D9 TEXT:"confidentially files"] for a U.S. IPO, edging ahead of rival OpenAI in a closely watched race to reach public markets. July 2026: A federal judge in San Francisco [USN:L6N41W171 TEXT:"signs off"] on Anthropic's landmark $1.5 billion settlement of a class-action lawsuit brought by a group of authors who accused it of misusing their books to train its AI chatbot Claude. August 2026: Independent music publisher Round Hill Music [USN:L6N44E0YF TEXT:"sues Anthropic"] and Suno in California federal court, alleging the AI companies misused hundreds of its songs to train their systems. August 2026: Anthropic is [USN:L6N4480X8 TEXT:"projecting 2028 revenue"] of roughly $190 billion to $200 billion, Reuters reports, citing sources. August 2026: Anthropic's annual revenue run rate [USN:L4N44E1B2 TEXT:"topped $65 billion"] by the end of July, Reuters reports, citing a source. October 2026: Reuters [USN:L6N4611F6 TEXT:"reported"], citing sources, that some current Anthropic investors and prospective investors in its upcoming IPO are weighing a lower valuation for the AI company after its latest financial disclosures. October 2026: Anthropic [USN:L1N46404R TEXT:"said"] it is planning one of the biggest IPOs in history as a public benefit corporation, a legal structure that requires management to balance broader public interests with profitability goals.
